title: Session stuck in "Starting" forever when the agent process hangs before the ACP handshake
description:
A session stuck in "starting" because its ACP transport process never exits
and never completes the `initialize` handshake hangs the winbar on "Starting"
forever, with no error, no timeout, and no way for the user to tell the
session is dead rather than slow.

## Observed

Live repro on 2026-08-30, agent config from ~/dotfiles' louiselm.lua:
`agents.opencode = { command = "acp-proxy", args = { "--", "opencode", "acp" } }`.

Real-world trigger: opencode CLI's npm postinstall script hadn't run, so
`opencode acp` exited immediately (exit 1, stderr message) without ever
speaking ACP. Selecting the opencode agent in Neovim left the winbar reading
"Starting" indefinitely with no error surfaced.

Synthetic repro isolating the mechanism (bypassing the opencode-specific
cause): wrapped a script that immediately fails with acp-proxy, the same way
louiselm does:

```
$ cat /tmp/fake-broken-agent.sh
#!/bin/sh
echo "Error: fake broken agent, postinstall never ran" >&2
exit 1

$ timeout 5 acp-proxy -- /tmp/fake-broken-agent.sh
Error: fake broken agent, postinstall never ran
# process is still running after the 5s timeout elapses; `timeout`'s SIGTERM
# has no effect. Confirmed via `ps aux`: the acp-proxy process (pid 433857)
# is still alive well after its wrapped child exited. Had to `kill -9` it.
```

`acp-proxy` (0.7.3, from ~/code/acp-llm-adapter) forwards the wrapped child's
stderr but does not exit or otherwise signal failure when that child dies
before the handshake completes — that is a separate defect, tracked in the
acp-llm-adapter repo, not here.

## Symptoms

- User sees the winbar's turn label stuck on "Starting" (rendered by
  `turn_label` at lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua:552-554 for
  `status == "starting"`) with no further change, ever.
- No error, no timeout message, nothing in the chat transcript.
- Nothing distinguishes "the agent process is slow to start" from "the agent
  process (or a proxy wrapping it) is permanently hung."

## Root cause

louiselm.nvim's own on_exit wiring is correct and not the bug: `Session:start`
(lua/louiselm/session/lifecycle.lua:660-676) passes `on_exit` through to
`Acp.connect`, which reaches `lua/louiselm/acp/transport.lua:112-125`'s
`on_exit`, which calls back into `handle_exit`
(lua/louiselm/session/lifecycle.lua:475-484), which calls `fail(...)` and
correctly flips `status` to `"error"` — *when the spawned process actually
exits*.

The gap is that nothing in the session lifecycle ever times out or health-checks
a session sitting in `"starting"`/`"configuring"` status. `vim.system`'s
on_exit callback is the *only* signal path out of "starting" besides a
successful `initialize` response
(`handle_initialized`, lifecycle.lua:489 onward). If the spawned process (here,
`acp-proxy` wrapping a dead child) never exits and never sends a handshake
response, there is no other exit condition — the session, and the winbar,
hang forever.

## Why it was not caught

No existing test exercises a spawned process that neither completes the ACP
handshake nor exits. The test suite's mock ACP agent (per AGENTS.md's testing
section) presumably always exits or always completes the handshake in its
fixtures — a permanently-silent, permanently-alive child was never modeled.

## Fix direction

Add a bounded startup timeout (e.g. via `vim.defer_fn` scheduled at
`Session:start()` and cancelled on `handle_initialized`/`handle_exit`) that
calls `fail(self, "agent did not respond within Ns of starting")` if the
session is still in `"starting"`/`"configuring"` when it fires. Options
rejected: relying solely on downstream proxies (acp-proxy, acp-llm-adapter) to
self-terminate correctly is not sufficient — louiselm spawns an arbitrary
user-configured command and cannot assume every wrapper behaves; a client-side
timeout is the only boundary louiselm fully controls.

## Acceptance

- A regression test that starts a session against a transport double which
  never calls its stdout/on_exit callbacks, and asserts the session
  transitions to `"error"` after the timeout rather than staying in
  `"starting"` indefinitely.
- Live: selecting an agent whose process hangs pre-handshake surfaces a
  timeout error in the transcript and updates the winbar, instead of leaving
  "Starting" displayed forever.

## Not covered

- The acp-proxy defect itself (not exiting/propagating when its wrapped child
  process dies) — tracked separately in ~/code/acp-llm-adapter's beads
  tracker, not here.
- Whether a configurable timeout duration is needed vs. a fixed default —
  left to implementation.
close_reason:
Fixed. Added a bounded startup timeout to Session:start() (lua/louiselm/session/lifecycle.lua):
after the ACP initialize request is sent, schedules a timer via a new testable
`self.schedule` boundary (defaults to vim.defer_fn, same pattern as
workflow/run.lua's `schedule` option). If the session is still "starting" when
the timer fires, it calls fail() with "agent did not respond within Nms of
starting" instead of hanging forever. Timeout defaults to
DEFAULT_START_TIMEOUT_MS = 20000, configurable per-session via the new
`start_timeout_ms` session option (validated and plumbed through
lua/louiselm/session/registry.lua's closed option schema).

Root cause confirmed as filed: acp-proxy (external dependency, tracked in
acp-llm-adapter as daa-yrsj, since fixed and rebuilt by the maintainer) never
exited when its wrapped child died pre-handshake, so louiselm's on_exit-based
detection never fired. This fix makes louiselm's own session lifecycle
self-bounding regardless of how a spawned process or proxy misbehaves,
matching the filed fix direction (a client-side timeout is the only boundary
louiselm fully controls).

Tests added in tests/session/api_spec.lua ("new" set):
- "fails a session that never completes the ACP handshake after the start
  timeout" - injects a captured schedule callback, fires it, asserts status
  transitions "starting" -> "error" with the expected message and that
  ready_callback receives the error.
- "ignores a stale start timeout after the Session becomes ready" - confirms
  the guard (status ~= "starting") prevents a late timer from clobbering an
  already-ready session.
- "honors a custom start_timeout_ms option" - asserts the configured value is
  what gets scheduled.
- "rejects a negative start_timeout_ms session option" - registry-level
  validation.

Gates: full mini.test suite (all files) - 0 fails, 0 notes.
`stylua --check` - clean. `lua-language-server --check . --checklevel=Warning`
- no problems found. `./scripts/generate-api-appendix --check` - regenerated
doc/api.md for the new public LuaCATS fields (schedule, start_timeout_ms,
stderr_buffer) and verified clean afterward.

Deviation: implementation was written before the regression tests rather than
strict red-green-refactor (tests were added and verified to exercise the new
code paths afterward, not proven red against pre-fix code first). Full test
suite is green and the new tests are behavioral (they'd fail against the
prior always-schedule-nothing behavior), but this is a self-report rather than
witnessed red-before-green.

title: Erasing a staged skill marker still invokes the skill
description:
Erasing a staged native skill's visible [context: skill: NAME] marker does not remove the selection. Submitting the remaining ordinary prompt still invokes that skill, although the editable prompt no longer shows it.

## Observed
Reported by the maintainer on 2026-09-09 in codex/01a08529-a75b-7202-96d4-b8d9ee4600cc after selecting ponytail-gain with <leader>sk. They do not remember whether they erased the marker. The logs cannot establish that editor action; do not claim that this particular turn proves marker deletion.

The exact submitted request is proven independently:
- /home/lotso/.local/state/acp-llm-adapter/proxy/sessions/01a08529-a75b-7202-96d4-b8d9ee4600cc/log.jsonl:2 advertises $ponytail-gain at 07:54:54.800Z.
- Same file:545 records client_to_agent session/prompt request 8 at 07:58:20.537Z. Its single text block starts with "/$ponytail-gain what's the diff in /home/lotso/.local/state/nvim/louiselm/"; no literal [context:...] marker was sent.
- /home/lotso/.codex/sessions/2026/09/09/rollout-2026-09-09T09-54-54-01a08529-a75b-7202-96d4-b8d9ee4600cc.jsonl:69 records the identical user text; :71 supplies the ponytail-gain skill body. This is the intended native invocation pipeline, not evidence of an adapter injecting an unrelated skill.

Separate reproduction against installed commit 739949f79a1f08995d743e3c2cf5b2208b80ecde confirms the deletion defect. An isolated headless Neovim loaded the installed Chat module, attached an in-memory ready native Session advertising $ponytail-gain, used the real skill picker with fed 1<CR> input, edited the prompt through nvim_buf_set_lines, and called Chat:submit() without an explicit text argument. No global/package monkey-patching or real Agent call was used. Child XDG_STATE_HOME was a temporary directory; live editor/state were untouched.

Observed outputs:
```json
{"removed_marker":false,"visible_before_submit":"> [context: skill: ponytail-gain] what's the diff in the state directories?","sent":"/$ponytail-gain what's the diff in the state directories?"}
{"removed_marker":true,"visible_before_submit":"> what's the diff in the state directories?","sent":"/$ponytail-gain what's the diff in the state directories?"}
```
Temporary reproduction artifact: /tmp/louiselm-skill-marker-3XfDir/repro.lua. The recipe and exact outputs above are the durable evidence if that temporary path expires.

## Root cause
lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua:1217 renders the chip and stores view.pending_skill independently. Its on_lines handler at :3308 only cancels queued_prompt; deleting a chip never reconciles pending_skill or contexts. Chat:submit at :4291 only strips the cached prefix if still present. build_content at :2070 unconditionally prepends the selected native command. clear_prompt_context at :2109 only runs at other lifecycle boundaries. The installed file has the same relevant code/line numbers.

## Why it was not caught
Existing tests/ui/chat_spec.lua cases cover native selection, command re-resolution, failed submission preservation, slash passthrough and one-time consumption. They do not select a skill, remove its visible marker through a buffer edit, then submit the buffer.

## Fix direction / acceptance
1. Deleting a staged skill marker must not silently submit the removed selection. Reconcile staged selection and its visible representation at the narrow shared boundary; do not merely strip the emitted /$ prefix after resolution.
2. Add a regression using real buffer edits and Chat:submit() with no explicit text. Selecting ponytail-gain, removing its entire marker and sending an ordinary prompt must send only that prompt. Keeping the marker must invoke the advertised skill once.
3. Preserve unrelated staged context, manual slash passthrough, failed-send retention, pending-command re-resolution, queued-prompt lifecycle and disposal. Exercise partial edits and native/injected context behavior where the chosen fix shares their boundary; do not silently drop unrelated content.
4. Run focused and full applicable Lua gates, then keep the live bug open until the maintainer repeats select -> erase marker -> ordinary prompt on the installed fix and confirms the skill is absent.

This was diagnosis only; no product code changed. The original keystroke sequence remains unknown. title: Gate demo layout with the to-be-continuous Playwright component
description:
## Problem Statement
The Interactive Demo layout regression currently runs manually. A future change can reintroduce page scrolling, clip tutorial controls, or leave the Neovim grid larger than its panel while the existing GitLab site checks pass.

## Solution
Use the existing to-be-continuous Playwright component in this repository's GitLab pipeline to test the generated site artifact and require a passing result before the existing manual deployment. Maintainer approved recording this approach as low-priority future work; do not implement as part of issue creation.

## User Stories
1. As the maintainer, I want browser layout regressions reported in merge requests before they reach the public demo.
2. As the maintainer, I want the established CI component to own test execution, caching and reports, with only project-specific configuration in this repository.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Reuse the mirrored to-be-continuous Playwright component, pinned to a reviewed immutable revision, and its playwright job. Preserve existing pipeline behavior outside the site checks.
2. Consume site-build's _build/html artifact and serve it locally with the cross-origin isolation headers required by Neovim WASM. Test the candidate artifact without deploying it or targeting the production website.
3. Run automatically as a required check for applicable branch/MR pipelines. Explicitly make site-deploy depend on successful browser checks; its existing manual deployment boundary remains.
4. Boot real Neovim for Core and Enhanced profiles in English and Simplified Chinese. Cover 10 guide steps plus completion at content viewport sizes 1920x1030, 1440x900 and 1280x720: 132 layout cases.
5. Assert no vertical/horizontal document overflow, all guide controls within their panel, guide above Neovim, editor bottom within the viewport, most vertical space allocated to Neovim, and rendered Neovim rows/columns fitting after resize.
6. Convert the existing CLI-driven regression into normal Playwright tests with reliable failure exit status and GitLab JUnit reports. Preserve deterministic visits to every guide state.
7. Pin the development-only @playwright/test package and matching browser image; keep these out of the published demo and Lua runtime dependencies.
8. Demonstrate a layout regression fails the CI check and prevents deployment; verify the corrected build passes.

## Implementation Notes
- Existing component mirror: https://gitlab.bartab.fr/to-be-continuous/playwright
- Inspected release: 1.10.0, commit c9ddc28361794d4103989501b6658f47f96236f3. Recheck the selected revision before integration.
- Upstream docs: https://to-be-continuous.gitlab.io/doc/ref/playwright/
- Component provides npm installation/cache, pre/post hooks, test invocation and JUnit artifacts. Its default acceptance/environment rules need scoped overrides for candidate artifact testing.
- Browser image contains browsers/system libraries, not the Playwright test package: https://playwright.dev/docs/docker
- Use Playwright webServer lifecycle support for the project-specific local artifact server.
- Reuse scripts/test-demo-layout.js from louiselm-q58u.10; avoid an additional bespoke CI runner or parallel duplicate suite.

## Testing Notes
Validate merged GitLab configuration, artifact transfer, job selection and the deployment dependency. Run the browser suite against the generated artifact with real asynchronous grid resize/redraw. Retain test evidence in GitLab reports.

## Out of Scope
Automating the full prompt/reject/accept/Resume/Handoff journey (the current layout regression uses Skip), production browser monitoring, changing deployment infrastructure, new review environments, and unrelated CI rewrites.

## Relationship
Follow-up to louiselm-q58u.10. CI integration is explicitly deferred here; it does not block the layout task's maintainer acceptance. No dependency edge is required.

title: myst build --html fails with ECONNREFUSED to its own localhost:3000 prerender server under Docker bridge networking
description:
`myst build --html --strict` (the exact command the new `.gitlab-ci.yml` pages job runs, on the exact `node:24-bookworm` image it pins) fails deterministically inside a plain `docker run` container using Docker's default bridge network, but succeeds on a bare host and succeeds inside the same container under `--network host`. This is an open risk for the real GitLab CI pipeline (louiselm-zce), unconfirmed because this sandbox has no live GitLab Runner to test against.

## Observed

Session: CI setup work for louiselm-zce (GitLab CI build+deploy of blog/ to GitLab Pages), 2026-08-18, in /home/lotso/code/louiselm sandbox with Docker 29.6.2 (overlayfs, cgroup v2, kernel 7.0.13+deb13-amd64).

Three reproductions of the identical command sequence `npm install -g mystmd@1.10.1 && cd blog && myst build --html --strict`:

1. Bare host, asdf-managed Node v24.16.0, no container: exit 0, `blog/_build/html/index.html` produced with real content. Ran twice, succeeded both times.
2. `docker run --rm -v <repo>:/repo -w /repo --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" node:24-bookworm bash -c '...'` with Docker's default bridge network (`docker network inspect bridge` shows `"EnableIPv6": false`, subnet `172.17.0.0/16`): exit 1, 3/3 runs. Build log (identical each time):
   ```
   🔌 Server started on port 3000!  🥳 🎉
   	👉  http://localhost:3000  👈
   Fetch of http://localhost:3000 threw an error (Attempt #1) FetchError: request to http://localhost:3000/ failed, reason: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:3000
   ... (repeats for /post-example/blog, /index.json, /post-example.blog.json, /robots.txt)
   Fetch of http://localhost:3000 threw an error (Attempt #2) ...
   Fetch of http://localhost:3000 threw an error (Attempt #3) ...
   Failed to fetch http://localhost:3000 after 3 attempts.
   Myst CLI Versions:
    - node                        24.19.0     Required: >= 18.0.0
    - npm                         11.17.0     Required: >=8.6.0
    - myst                         1.10.1
   ```
3. Same container/command but `docker run --network host ...`: exit 0, 1/1 run, full successful build log with `GET / 200`, `GET /post-example/blog 200`, etc.

Root cause is unknown — not simple loopback breakage: a minimal manual repro in the same bridge-mode container (`node -e "http.createServer(...).listen(4000, () => fetch('http://localhost:4000/'))"`) succeeded fine, both with default `::` bind and explicit `127.0.0.1` bind. So the failure is specific to mystmd's book-theme dev-server startup path under bridge networking, not a blanket "loopback fetch doesn't work" issue.

## Symptoms

- What a CI job running this exact command inside a Docker-executor container with default (bridge) networking might see: the `myst build --html --strict` step fails with exit 1 and the pipeline job goes red, even though nothing about the blog content is broken.
- Error text: `FetchError: request to http://localhost:3000/ failed, reason: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:3000`, followed by `Failed to fetch http://localhost:3000 after 3 attempts.`

## Root cause

Unknown. Hypotheses, not yet discriminated:

1. Docker bridge-mode NAT/userland-proxy hairpin latency delays the container's own published port becoming reachable via `localhost`, and mystmd's book-theme prerender step's 3 retries (short interval, not measured) aren't enough margin under that added latency — would be a timing/robustness gap in mystmd's book-theme server startup (fixed asynchronously logs "started" possibly before actually ready to accept), not a hard capability gap.
2. Something specific to this sandboxed/nested-Docker environment's bridge network implementation (this sandbox is itself a constrained/virtualized environment) that would NOT reproduce on a normal cloud VM running a normal GitLab Docker-executor runner.

Nothing in this investigation distinguishes between these two. A real GitLab Runner is required to know which applies.

## Why it was not caught

There is no automated CI yet (this bug was found while building the very first `.gitlab-ci.yml` for this repo) and no live GitLab Runner reachable from this sandbox, so the only verification possible was local reproduction of the exact command/image, which surfaced this discrepancy but can't confirm whether it will recur on the real runner.

## Fix direction

Do not speculatively patch `.gitlab-ci.yml` for this (e.g. forcing host networking isn't controllable from `.gitlab-ci.yml` — it's a GitLab Runner `config.toml` `[runners.docker] network_mode` setting, out of this repo's control). Instead:

1. Watch the first real pipeline run of the `pages` job (in `.gitlab-ci.yml`, already carries an inline comment flagging this) for the exact `ECONNREFUSED ... :3000` signature during the `myst build` step.
2. If it recurs on the real runner: escalate to whoever administers the GitLab Runner to check/change the Docker executor's `network_mode`, or file upstream against `jupyter-book/mystmd` (book-theme prerender retry/backoff robustness).
3. If it does NOT recur: close this as sandbox-environment-specific and not a real risk.

## Acceptance

- A real GitLab CI pipeline run of the `pages` job in `.gitlab-ci.yml` either succeeds (closes this as sandbox-specific noise) or reproduces the same `ECONNREFUSED :3000` signature (confirms the risk and triggers the escalation above).

## Not covered

- Whether GitLab.com shared runners vs. this project's actual self-hosted `gitlab.bartab.fr` runner(s) would behave differently — runner topology for `gitlab.bartab.fr` is unknown from this sandbox.
- Whether pinning a different Node major (e.g. `node:20-bookworm`, `node:22-bookworm`) avoids the issue — not tested; the discrepancy was isolated to bridge-vs-host Docker networking, not Node version, so this seems unlikely to matter but wasn't ruled out.
close_reason: Confirmed on real gitlab.bartab.fr pipeline #38205: HOST=127.0.0.1 CI variable fixes the ECONNREFUSED. Root cause was mystmd's dev server binding to hostname 'localhost' racing IPv4/IPv6 resolution under Docker bridge networking.

comments.author: 3869f178-9bdd-4a0f-981c-2b01567e1e60
comments.text:
Confirmed on the real gitlab.bartab.fr runner: identical ECONNREFUSED signature on 4/4 pipeline runs (2026-08-19 through 2026-08-22, pipelines #37950/#37998/#38076/#38120), so this is real, not sandbox-specific.

Root cause pinned down: mystmd's book-theme dev server (myst-cli/dist/build/site/start.js) binds via `app.listen(port, host)` with `DEFAULT_HOST='localhost'` (a hostname, not an IP). Under this runner's Docker bridge network (IPv6 disabled per the original bead's `docker network inspect`), resolving `localhost` races IPv4/IPv6 and the self-fetch prerender step hits ECONNREFUSED on the unreachable family before its 3-attempt/exponential-backoff retry (`fetchWithRetry`, ~750ms total budget) gives up. Confirmed via mystmd's own escape hatch: it already special-cases this exact failure for ReadTheDocs by forcing `HOST=127.0.0.1` (`warnOnHostEnvironmentVariable` in myst-cli). Setting `HOST=127.0.0.1` as a CI variable reproduced success 3/3 times locally in the same bridge-mode `docker run node:24-bookworm` setup that previously failed 3/3.

Fix applied: added `variables: HOST: "127.0.0.1"` to the `pages` job in `.gitlab-ci.yml`. No runner infra change needed (network_mode stays default bridge, group-wide runner untouched) — chosen over changing the runner's network_mode specifically, to keep blast radius to this one job.

Next: watch the next real pipeline run (triggered by this commit) to confirm the fix holds under the actual runner, then close.

comments.author: 3869f178-9bdd-4a0f-981c-2b01567e1e60
comments.text: Confirmed fixed: pipeline #38205 (triggered by commit 60f1e0f) passed with the HOST=127.0.0.1 CI variable in place. Closing.

title: Parallelize skills-core CI privileged test step across jobs
description:
The `cargo (skills-core)` CI job takes ~14 minutes wall time, and one step —
"Test measured Agent and isolated tool grants" — accounts for 9m4s of it
(run 34958590297, job 104346492180, 2026-09-15). That step runs ~14 sequential
`sudo`-privileged sub-tests in a single shell block
(.github/workflows/ci.yml:466-505): tool isolation, grant execution, broker
launch effects, receipt history rotation, socket activation across restart,
control daemon under `unshare --mount` (timeout 240), a broker-systemd Python
test, a 4-scenario cold-resume loop (each capped at timeout 240), launch
failures, exact job verification, and certification under `unshare --net`
(timeout 200).

These tests self-skip in under a second when their gating `LOUISELM_REQUIRE_*`
env var is unset (e.g. tool_integration_tests.rs:127), which is why this never
shows up locally -- `./scripts/test-skills-core` / the documented local
workflow never sets those vars, so the ~9-minute path is CI-exclusive.

Proposal: split that step into separate parallel CI jobs, one per privileged
sub-test or logical group (the cold-resume loop is the obvious first split:
4 independent scenarios already self-timed via `TIMEFORMAT`). This repo
already runs ~12 jobs concurrently in the same workflow without issue, so the
pattern is established. Splitting across jobs (not backgrounding within one
runner) matters because these tests reserve a shared fixture uid (60000),
systemd units, and cgroup paths -- safe when each gets its own fresh runner
VM, not obviously safe run concurrently inside one.

Tradeoff to weigh before implementing: each new job pays fixed per-job
overhead (checkout, apt-get install bubblewrap/strace, rustup install --
about 35-40s today) and, unless a shared warm `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` is restored
via `actions/cache`, redundant incremental compilation of the
`louiselm_skills` lib/bins per job. On a metered private-repo Actions plan
that's a real CI-minutes cost increase in exchange for shorter wall time -- a
premium worth pricing, not assumed free.

Not yet measured: per-sub-test timing within the 9m4s block (only the
aggregate is known). Before splitting, instrument each `sudo env ... --exact`
invocation with `time` (or reuse the existing cold-resume
`TIMEFORMAT`/`time` pattern) to find which sub-tests are actually the long
poles, so the job split targets real weight rather than an even guess.

No existing issue covers this (checked `br search -a` for "skills-core CI
slow" and "cold resume" -- only louiselm-afrki, an unrelated cold-resume
correctness bug).
notes: Investigation first (maintainer request 2026-09-18). Acceptance: (1) break down several representative CI runs into setup/cache/build/test/scenario timings and explain observed 18–27 minute variation; (2) compare the same enabled privileged suite in a disposable local guest versus CI, documenting skipped gates and runner resources, rather than comparing plain cargo tests or release-only fixtures; (3) identify repeated fixture setup, serial shared-identity constraints, hashing and waits using evidence; (4) evaluate isolated job groups, cached/build-artifact reuse and change-scoped CI as candidates, reporting expected wall time, total runner minutes, overhead and coverage/trigger risks; (5) recommend the smallest measured improvement and file execution-ready follow-ups if implementation is separate. Do not run privileged fixtures on maintainer host, background shared UID/systemd/cgroup fixtures together, weaken security assertions, or skip required exact-release-commit coverage. Parallelization in original description remains a hypothesis to assess, not a required conclusion. Prior lesson: louiselm-cjpep (measured executable debug metadata/hashing). Investigation alone does not change CI or claim a speedup.

title: Reach historical backlog state by git ref for decision vintage
description:
## Goal

Reach the state of the backlog as it was at a given commit, so a past decision
can be re-read against what was known when it was made.

## Scope

- In scope: `lua/louiselm/provenance/vintage.lua`; resolving a git ref to the
  historical `.beads/issues.jsonl`; a diff between that state and now; surfacing
  it in the issue Provenance view for a closed question.
- Out of scope: judging whether a decision still holds. This slice supplies
  evidence, not opinion.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Given a git ref, return the backlog state at that ref and the difference
   from the current state.
2. The upstream defect is encapsulated here and nowhere else, behind an
   interface stable enough that the module can be deleted wholesale once
   upstream is fixed, without touching callers.
3. A ref with no `.beads/issues.jsonl`, and a ref that predates the file, both
   fail with actionable errors rather than a misleading one.

## Testing

- A temporary git repository fixture with a committed `.beads/issues.jsonl`,
  including the custom-status case, so the workaround has a red test proving why
  it exists and a signal for when it can be removed.
- A test that fails once upstream starts working, so the workaround cannot
  quietly outlive its cause.

## Notes

Blocked in practice by louiselm-f8r1, which the maintainer has deferred
upstream: bvr rejects every custom-status record, so its git-ref path fails
outright on this backlog and its lenient path silently drops all ten
vocabulary records.

The workaround is to extract the snapshot first and use the file-path form.
Note honestly that this addresses only the hard-failure half; the dropped
vocabulary records remain dropped, so any metric computed from a historical
snapshot is computed over an incomplete corpus until upstream is fixed.
close_reason: Implemented historical backlog extraction and closed-Decision drift rendering; 732 tests and all quality gates pass.

comments.text: Implemented the contained workaround. provenance.vintage parses historical .beads/issues.jsonl directly via git show, preserves custom-status records, compares against the current file by issue ID, and reports missing historical snapshots with git detail. Closed-question Provenance uses the recorded closing commit as the historical ref and renders issue count plus added/removed/changed drift. Regression coverage: tests/provenance/vintage_spec.lua and tests/ui/provenance_spec.lua. Lesson: keep this extraction boundary isolated so it can be deleted when bvr supports git refs; do not route historical snapshots through bvr, which drops custom statuses.

title: Witness tests inherit personal Git signing configuration
description:
The skills-core witness tests inherit personal Git signing configuration and can invoke the operator's GPG signer instead of remaining credential-free.

## Observed
2026-09-08 C14 fixes, codex/01a07d34-4adb-7491-8d0a-3f23cd0796e1. Full suite via systemd user service run-p536300-i534469, invocation4b88b7b00f1b4ef384eebfdb102e7a4a, using scripts/test-skills-core and inherited PATH. Library106 PASS/2 existing ignored; admission18 PASS/1 FAIL:
tests/admission.rs:208 a_generation_becomes_current_only_after_the_exact_bytes_are_witnessed: Witness(Git { command: "commit", reason: "error: gpg failed to sign the data ... gpg: signing failed: Cannot allocate memory ... fatal: failed to write commit object" }).
No signature success or private-key read observed; public key identifier omitted. Test remote is disposable/local, not GitHub.

## Symptoms
Personal commit.gpgsign affects an ostensibly credential-free test; full gate fails and may prompt for personal signing depending on environment.

## Root cause
src/witness.rs:126-130 initializes scratch Git repository and author identity; :140-150 inherits Git configuration/environment; :218-220 commits without fixture signing isolation. tests/support/mod.rs:118 creates a local bare remote but does not isolate personal Git configuration for the witness client's scratch repositories. scripts/test-skills-core only closes runner FDs. The systemd workaround for louiselm-2fb5 also drops caller environment except explicitly forwarded fields.

## Why it was not caught
Ordinary local runs/CI lack the triggering personal signing config or inherit environment overrides that suppress it. Tests exercise real Git, but do not establish a hermetic Git config boundary.

## Fix direction
Isolate test Git configuration at the fixture/runner boundary; do not disable production witness signing or edit the operator's Git configuration. Use process-local GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null and GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1 for this gate rerun. Avoid any real signer retry.

## Acceptance
- Regression with a synthetic signing-enabled config/fake signer demonstrates failure before fixture isolation.
- Full tests succeed without invoking the fake/personal signer, touching real key material or changing host Git config.
- Production witness/remote authority semantics remain unchanged.

## Not covered
Deferred: outside the two authorized passkey fixes. Recorded before further gate execution. No change to witness code, global Git config, keys or GPG agent; only test-process environment isolation for current verification. Exact GPG memory refusal mechanism not diagnosed.
close_reason: Test launcher isolates inherited Git config; synthetic signer regression and full Rust gates pass. gate:scripts/test-skills-core-git-isolation

title: Grill-me needed: What should a Handoff carry instead of the full rendered transcript?
description:
Do not resolve this design question in passing. Facilitate a dedicated decision about what payload a Handoff injects into the receiving Session.

Question:
What should a Handoff carry? The shipped payload is the full rendered transcript markdown, and a real Handoff of that exact shape just drove the receiving Agent into a 52-turn no-progress loop that the maintainer interrupted twice. The maintainer's hypothesis: sending the full transcript of the conversation is why the receiver spun. Decide what is injected — full transcript, a compacted summary, a typed context block, a reference to the source Session — and how the receiver is framed so it consumes the payload as context instead of replaying it as its own conversation.

Evidence from shared conversation:
- On 2026-08-27 the maintainer handed off `claude/161e0a06-dea4-471b-99de-caa1ea641212` (session limit hit) to a new deepseek Session: `deepseek/session-39731cb4-4de6-49c9-8c14-c8c55bf06df6` (deepseek-v4-flash, reasoning high, yolo).
- The Handoff injected the full transcript: the receiver's first user message is 266,953 characters, starting with the renderer's own header "# louiselm session transcript - session: session-1 - agent: claude - acp session: 161e0a06…". It contains every User/Assistant/Reasoning turn and every Tool entry with its full raw payload (`nvim.inspect(raw)`), including whole file contents read during the source session.
- The receiver never completed anything. Its persisted history shows 52 assistant turns, ~104 `run_command` calls, overwhelmingly repeated state re-verification (`git status --short && echo "---DIFF---" && git diff --stat`, `br sync --flush-only`, `git log --oneline`) with prose such as "Let me check the current state of the working tree and beads, then commit and sync." The maintainer interrupted it twice; it kept spinning the same cycle.
- Plausible trigger: the transcript tail ended mid-task ("ok commit and sync" plus the still-open "thinking still not appears" investigation), so the receiver inherited pending work, kept re-checking state, and never acted — while the payload itself gave it 267KB of extra conversation to keep re-reading.
- Mechanics: `Chat:hand_off()` → `new_session(target)` → `open_handoff()` renders `Transcript.render(transcript snapshot, state)` (`lua/louiselm/session/transcript.lua:272`) into an editable markdown review buffer → `submit_handoff()` sends the buffer text verbatim as the receiving Session's first prompt (`lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua:2786-2863`). The transcript is shaped for human review, then consumed by a model as conversation.
- The renderer already knows raw payload inlines can corrupt its own format: tool payloads are fenced because a `##` line inside one fabricates a section indistinguishable from the format's own (louiselm-cmr, `transcript.lua` module comment). Human-readable markdown is load-bearing for the model here, and it has no structural boundary between "record of the source conversation" and "instructions to you".
- The maintainer's proposed direction, recorded verbatim from the conversation that raised this: "markdown is meant for humans, maybe a [context: transcript] would be better to avoid falling into that loop trap."
- Canonical vocabulary (louiselm-7rjr, Handoff) defines Handoff as "creation of a Session with another Agent, including injection of a reviewed transcript while retaining the source Session" — so changing what is injected may require updating that reference record.

Threads worth pulling:
- What is a Handoff's job: transfer enough state for the receiver to continue in-progress work, or give it context to answer a fresh question? This incident mixed both (limit hit mid-task, no new instruction given). Do the two jobs need different payloads, and should the operator be forced to state which one a Handoff is?
- Should the payload carry an explicit instruction block to the receiver ("you are taking over: commit and sync, then verify X"), separate from the context, so the receiver has a task instead of inferring one from a transcript tail?
- Payload shape: full markdown transcript vs a compacted summary (decisions, open threads, pending commands, dirty-tree state, next step) vs the maintainer's typed envelope — e.g. a `[context: transcript]` block mirroring the `[resource] <louiselm://…>` and skills-index blocks louiselm already injects into prompts — vs no transcript at all, only a reference to the source ACP session id that the receiver loads on demand (the deepseek adapter advertises `load_session`).
- Fidelity: what must survive a Handoff (decisions, open questions, pending commands, uncommitted state) and what is safe to drop (raw tool payloads, Reasoning blocks)? Should tool entries elide to title + status, the way the human renderer already truncates captions at 120 characters?
- Review step: the editable markdown buffer is the operator's review/edit affordance before submit. If the payload becomes machine-readable, where does human review happen — on the summary only, with the full record kept behind a pointer?
- Loop attribution: is the loop primarily payload size (a 267KB first message dwarfing the real task), framing (transcript presented as conversation-to-continue rather than context-to-consume), or model/params (flash + max-token config)? What evidence would separate these — and should louiselm add a no-progress guard (repeated identical tool invocations → park/notify) independent of the payload answer?
- Whether changing the injected payload requires promoting an updated Handoff vocabulary record (louiselm-7rjr), per the vocabulary promotion rules.

Decision boundary:
Choose what a Handoff injects and how it frames the receiver. Do not design a no-progress loop guard here unless the evidence shows payload shape alone cannot prevent the loop; provider/agent switching and source-Session mutation stay out of scope as today.
close_reason: Design settled with the maintainer: takeover-brief + compacted-context handoff payload, typed resource transport with text fallback. Vocabulary louiselm-7rjr promoted; implementation filed as louiselm-mtte; forensics capability misread filed as louiselm-7nod.

comments.author: deepseek/session-10e3f0c1-f72e-4107-90c6-6af1d3eed3aa
comments.text:
Resolved with the maintainer, 2026-08-27 (grill in deepseek/session-10e3f0c1).

Decision: a Handoff is always a takeover. The payload becomes (1) a mandatory operator-authored ## Handoff section (source, takeover task template, optional constraints) that submit refuses to send while blank; (2) a ## Context section carrying the compacted transcript — user prompts and assistant prose kept, tools reduced to title+status, reasoning blocks and repeated injected resource text dropped; (3) a ## Source section. Transport: the Context travels as an ACP resource block (louiselm://handoff/<source-id>, text/markdown) when the target advertises promptCapabilities.embeddedContext, else flattened into the text prompt; reuses the existing build_content branch. Estimated effect on the incident: 267KB -> ~20-25KB with the task first.

Rejected, with reasons:
- Full transcript (status quo): the incident itself.
- Source-agent-authored summary at handoff time: takeover happens precisely when the source session is exhausted (limit/error), so it cannot be the author.
- Cross-agent loadSession pointer only: impossible — loadSession is per-Agent; the deepseek receiver cannot load a claude session.
- Plain-text-only envelope: replaced once louiselm-7nod showed the Forensics embedded_context=false read was a misread; the deepseek adapter advertises and handles embedded resources. The framing label [resource] <uri> is accepted; backend-side message-role separation deferred out of scope.
- No-progress loop guard: out of this question's boundary; file separately if evidence warrants.

Routes: Handoff vocabulary promoted (louiselm-7rjr), implementation filed as louiselm-mtte (depends on this issue), Forensics capability misread filed as louiselm-7nod.

title: No production process runs the Control broker
description:
## Evidence

Nothing in production constructs the Control broker.

- `InstalledBroker::bind` has exactly one non-test caller,
  `skills-core/src/broker/installed.rs:214`, and no binary reaches it.
  `grep bind skills-core/src/bin/*.rs` is empty.
- `BrokerService::bind` appears only under `tests/` and `*_tests.rs`.
- `louiselm-launch` calls `connect_control_broker(&config, BROKER_TIMEOUT)`
  against `config.broker_socket_path` (`/run/louiselm/control.sock`), so the
  launcher expects something already listening there.
- There is no service unit for it. `contrib/systemd/` ships units for ACP backup
  and capture-service only; `launcher_install.rs` provisions the socket *path*
  and its permissions, never a process.

So the broker is a library that tests and the privileged VM gates instantiate
in-process. In production the socket has no listener.

## Why it matters

Every broker capability built so far — lifecycle authority, recovery admission,
Attention projection, and now `session_status` — is unreachable in production
for this one reason. It is the difference between the components being
individually correct and the system existing, which is exactly the inert-green
failure `louiselm-d6fv.9` was written against.

It also blocks `louiselm-qbr.5.1.2.4.1`: an operator CLI needs a broker process
to ask, and there is none. That slice was filed assuming the missing piece was
an operator endpoint; the missing piece is the whole daemon.

## Scope

- In scope: a supervised broker process that binds the installed rendezvous;
  its service unit and installation provisioning; startup ownership/permission
  checks; restart behaviour against the existing `serve_reconnect` reattachment
  contract; shutdown that does not strand unresolved lifecycle intents.
- Out of scope: new broker capabilities. This runs what already exists.

## Open question

Whether this belongs inside `louiselm-d6fv.9`'s cutover or stands alone. Filed
separately because `d6fv.9` reads as an operator migration, and nothing in it
names the missing process.

Production broker daemon, provisioning, identity continuity, Attention and explicit audited adoption have consumers and passing owning/installed VM gates. Lessons in docs/broker-lifecycle.md. consumer:skills-core/src/bin/louiselm-control.rs:45

Covered by tests/broker/reconnect.rs one_rendezvous_routes_... Contract in docs/broker-lifecycle.md.

Why this was needed first: both existing entry points accepted a connection and then demanded a specific opening packet, so neither could serve a live rendezvous. A running broker cannot know which is arriving.

Remaining, and larger than a serve loop because it is an installation change to a privileged boundary:
1. louiselm-control serve binary. The component name is already reserved in release::ALLOWED_COMPONENTS; a client verb for qbr.5.1.2.4.1 can share it.
2. Broker-owned state directory. InstalledBroker::bind requires private_directory(state, broker_uid, broker_gid) at mode 0700, and nothing in launcher_install.rs provisions one. There is no state path in LauncherPaths at all.

title: Adopt a systemd-provided listening socket
description:
## Goal
Let the broker serve a listening `SOCK_SEQPACKET` socket created by systemd instead of binding its own.

## Decisions this implements
Confirmed in louiselm-crjt (2026-09-14): the rendezvous is provisioned by a systemd `.socket` unit, and the broker asserts `SO_PASSCRED` itself rather than trusting `PassCredentials=` in unit configuration. A security-critical setting sourced from an unvalidated external file is the failure mode this project keeps repeating; applying it on adoption makes it true because the code made it true.

## Scope
- In scope: a public `SeqpacketListener` constructor adopting an inherited fd; `LISTEN_FDS`/`LISTEN_PID` parsing refusing anything but exactly one fd meant for this process; `configure_passcred` and `configure_packet_buffers` applied to the adopted fd; a `BrokerService`/`InstalledBroker` constructor taking the adopted listener.
- Out of scope: the daemon loop, the units, provisioning.

## Notes
`SeqpacketListener::from_listening(fd)` already exists privately in `skills-core/src/launch_transport.rs:821` and is the adoption primitive; it does not currently configure the socket.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. An inherited listening fd is adopted and serves connections identically to a self-bound listener.
2. `SO_PASSCRED` is set by this code on the adopted fd; peer-credential checks work without any unit-file setting.
3. Wrong `LISTEN_PID`, zero fds, more than one fd, a non-socket fd, and a non-`SOCK_SEQPACKET` socket are each refused with a typed error.
4. The existing self-binding path keeps working unchanged for tests.

title: Detect broker state identity drift with a durable marker
description:
## Goal
Detect that the broker's durable state changed owning identity, and fail closed when it does.

## Why this is needed
Confirmed in louiselm-crjt (2026-09-14). systemd `StateDirectory=` recursively chowns an existing state directory to match the unit's `User=` whenever they differ (verified against systemd 257 `systemd.exec`). That silently repairs exactly the drift `private_directory` exists to catch, making its ownership check vacuous. A recorded marker is strictly stronger than a uid check: a uid check sees only the current owner, a marker sees that the owner *changed*.

This protects the claim that the state is this broker's private state. It does not protect integrity — receipts are signed and `verified_chain` validates them, so re-owning the directory forges nothing.

## Scope
- In scope: write a durable identity marker into the broker state directory at first bind; verify it on every later bind; refuse with a typed, actionable error naming the adoption verb when it does not match.
- Out of scope: the adoption verb itself (sibling task), unit files.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. First bind on an empty state directory writes the marker and succeeds.
2. A later bind with a matching marker succeeds and does not rewrite it.
3. A bind whose marker names a different identity refuses with a typed error that names the next safe action; no state is read or modified.
4. A missing marker beside existing broker state is refused, not silently adopted.
5. A torn or malformed marker fails closed.

title: Run the Control broker as louiselm-control serve
description:
## Goal
Run the Control broker as a process: `louiselm-control serve`.

## Decisions this implements
Confirmed in louiselm-crjt (2026-09-14). State is `/var/lib/louiselm/broker`, broker-owned 0700, on machine lifetime. The process adopts a systemd-provided socket (96pv.1) and checks the identity marker (96pv.2).

Shutdown does not drain. Stop accepting, close session channels, exit promptly, and rely on durable-before-acknowledge plus `serve_reconnect` reattachment. Draining would duplicate a tested mechanism inside a bounded stop timeout it does not control, and a path that only runs under time pressure is where the bugs live. A clean stop is therefore [[Broker loss]] to every live Session.

## Scope
- In scope: the `serve` verb on the `louiselm-control` binary (name already reserved in `release::ALLOWED_COMPONENTS`); the accept loop calling `InstalledBroker::serve_connection`; one worker per accepted Session driving `InstalledBroker::step` until it reports terminal; SIGTERM handling that stops accepting and exits without acknowledging anything not already durable.
- Out of scope: Attention delivery (sibling), unit files (sibling), the `adopt-state` verb (sibling), any client verb.

## Notes
`serve_connection` (a5fc8c2) already routes a connection by its first packet, so one loop serves both new launches and post-restart reattachments. `InstalledBroker::bind` already refuses to run unless the process is `broker_uid`/`broker_gid` with no supplementary groups.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. `louiselm-control serve` binds nothing itself, adopts the inherited socket, and serves a launch end to end.
2. A supervisor reattaching after the process restarts is reattached on the same rendezvous.
3. One misbehaving or failed Session does not stop the accept loop or affect another Session's worker.
4. SIGTERM stops accepting and exits within the stop timeout; no receipt is acknowledged that was not already durable.
5. Refuses to start when not the configured broker identity, when state fails `private_directory`, or when the marker mismatches.

title: Deliver queued Attention from the running broker
description:
## Goal
Drain the broker's durable Attention outbox to capture-service while the broker runs.

## Why it is separate
Confirmed in louiselm-crjt (2026-09-14): this requirement is why the broker is an always-running service rather than socket-activated on demand. If the broker only started when a supervisor dialled, queued Attention would sit undelivered whenever no Session happened to be connecting — which is most of the time, and Attention is the point of the qbr epic.

## Scope
- In scope: a delivery worker owned by the running broker calling `InstalledBroker::deliver_attention` with the `AttentionEndpoint`; bounded retry that leaves the oldest entry pending until its exact sequence/digest acknowledgement is durable; clean stop with the process.
- Out of scope: projection semantics, capture-service changes, Android delivery.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Entries enqueued while the broker runs are delivered without a Session connecting.
2. Entries enqueued before start are delivered after start.
3. Delivery failure retries without dropping, reordering, or duplicating the pending entry, and never changes authorization or receipts.
4. A capture-service outage does not stop the accept loop or any Session worker.
5. The worker stops with the process without acknowledging an undelivered entry.

title: Install the broker socket and service units
description:
## Goal
Ship the systemd units that provision and run the broker, and state the contract they now own.

## Decisions this implements
Confirmed in louiselm-crjt (2026-09-14).

- `louiselm-broker.socket`: enabled, `ListenSequentialPacket=/run/louiselm/control.sock`, `SocketMode=0600`. `RuntimeDirectory=louiselm` with `RuntimeDirectoryMode=0700` belongs on **this** unit, not the service — putting it on the service would delete `/run/louiselm` out from under the socket systemd is still listening on.
- `louiselm-broker.service`: `WantedBy=multi-user.target`, always running, `StateDirectory=louiselm/broker`, `StateDirectoryMode=0700`, `User=`/`Group=` the dedicated broker identity, `Restart=on-failure` with a short `RestartSec` so a crash reattaches well inside a typical grace window.

Verified against systemd 257: for a nested `StateDirectory`, only the innermost directory is chowned, so `/var/lib/louiselm` stays root-owned and satisfies both `private_directory`'s ancestor rule and the existing `ensure_root_directory(..., 0o711, false)` check. The two provisioners do not conflict in either order.

Note this is a **system** unit. The only existing systemd precedent, `capture-service/contrib/systemd/louiselm-capture.service`, is a `--user` unit running as the operator and cannot be copied: `louiselm-qbr.5.1` AC4 requires the broker to share neither operator nor capture-service identity.

## Also in scope: two contract statements
1. `BrokerService::close`'s doc comment currently claims "the installer owns the rendezvous path's lifetime". That has never been true — nothing provisions it today. Replace it with the invariant the code actually backs: whoever provisions must satisfy `private_directory`, which is re-checked on every start.
2. Record in `docs/broker-lifecycle.md` that one Control broker serves exactly one operator identity, already enforced by `InstalledBroker::authorize` and `LifecycleCaller::Operator`. If multi-operator is ever wanted it is N instances with separate identities, sockets and state — not one partitioned broker.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Starting the socket unit creates `/run/louiselm` broker-owned at 0700 and the socket at 0600.
2. Starting the service creates `/var/lib/louiselm/broker` broker-owned at 0700, leaving `/var/lib/louiselm` root-owned.
3. `bind` accepts both paths; stopping and restarting the service leaves the socket in place and reattaches.
4. `close`'s comment states the invariant, not an owner. The single-operator constraint is recorded.
5. Units are covered by whatever installed/VM gate covers the other privileged boundaries; report honestly if that gate cannot run here.

title: Adopt broker state after a deliberate identity change
description:
## Goal
Give the operator a supported, recorded way past an identity-marker refusal.

## Why this exists
Confirmed in louiselm-crjt (2026-09-14). The enemy is *silent* adoption, not adoption. A refusal with no door does not prevent the bad outcome — the operator hits a broker that will not start and reaches for `rm -rf /var/lib/louiselm/broker`, destroying the receipt chain the marker existed to protect. Loud, deliberate and attributable beats impossible.

Safe because receipts are signed and `verified_chain` validates them independently of directory ownership; adoption re-owns, it does not forge.

## Scope
- In scope: `louiselm-control adopt-state`; explicit operator confirmation; re-stamping the marker; a new `AuditDecision` variant recording the previous and new identity so the adoption is checkable by someone other than whoever ran it.
- Out of scope: automatic adoption in any form, recovery from a missing or corrupt receipt chain.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Run against a mismatched marker, it re-stamps and writes the audit entry; the next `serve` starts.
2. Run against a matching marker it is a no-op and says so; it never rewrites a valid marker.
3. It refuses unless invoked by the configured operator identity.
4. The audit entry names the previous and new identity and survives restart.
5. No path re-stamps the marker without this verb being run.
close_reason: Explicit operator adoption is wired into the measured installed CLI; audited replacement, no-op, refusals, receipt preservation and daemon restart pass the disposable VM gate and full Rust gates. Lesson in docs/broker-lifecycle.md. consumer:skills-core/src/bin/louiselm-control.rs:59

Hold an exclusive directory lock across installed daemon lifetime and adoption. Write durable machine-scoped AuditDecision before atomic marker publication; record explicitly proves authorized intent, not completion by itself. Matching marker is a no-op; missing/corrupt markers remain refused; receipt bytes and verification remain untouched. Acceptance: focused identity/CLI regressions, actual installed daemon refusal/adoption/restart in disposable VM, full owning gates.

comments.text: Implemented exact adopt-state --confirm verb, verified installed release/broker account, canonical sudo operator attribution, offline directory locking, durable machine-scoped StateIdentityAdoption intent before atomic marker replacement, matching no-op and explicit refusals. Manual sudo only; no installed privilege grant or receipt rewrite. Full skills-core suite passes (46.674s, /tmp/louiselm-96pv-verified-tests.log); fmt, strict Clippy, Rustdoc, browser 13/13 and diff checks pass. Final installed-daemon VM gate passes (58.40s, /tmp/louiselm-96pv-vm-daemon.log): real sudo invocation, wrong/missing operator and confirmation refusal, audit persistence, exact receipt preservation, no-op, restart and active-state refusal. Initial VM attempts exposed invocation umask and fixture-only sudo permission gaps; final harness matches CI umask022 and grants only the disposable test command inside private mounts. Lesson: adoption audit proves intent before publication, not completion; matching retry resyncs durability without rewriting. Documented docs/broker-lifecycle.md. Lock race tracked/fixed in 96pv.6.1. No host deployment or commit requested.

title: Adoption lock can survive return in concurrently forked children
description: Evidence: /tmp/louiselm-96pv-final-tests.log, full parallel skills-core suite, broker::state_identity::tests::explicit_adoption_preserves_receipts_and_audits_before_restarting failed on immediate matching adoption with StateInUse after successful first adoption. File close releases flock only after every inherited descriptor closes; concurrent subprocess fork can temporarily retain the open file description before exec despite CLOEXEC. Adoption currently relies only on File drop. Release the adoption lock explicitly on success and error before returning; preserve typed unlock errors. A live daemon must continue holding its own lock for its lifetime.
close_reason: Explicit unlock on adoption success/error prevents fork-inherited flock from surviving return; full parallel suite passes. Lesson recorded in issue. gate:skills-core/src/broker/state_identity.rs

Full parallel skills-core suite now passes (/tmp/louiselm-96pv-verified-tests.log, 46.674s). Lesson stays here: CLOEXEC closes at exec, not fork, so File drop alone can briefly retain flock through an inherited descriptor. Installed daemon continues holding its lock for its full lifetime.

title: Show historical Decision evidence and drift
description:
## Goal
Let a maintainer revisit a Decision using the backlog and evidence that existed when it was made, plus explicit later drift.

## Scope
- In scope: a read-only historical Decision view combining the closing commit, Beads snapshot at that commit, changes since, transcript resolution, and explicit reconsideration/supersession relations.
- Out of scope: fixing bvr, judging whether a Decision was wrong, copying transcripts, and a graph visualization.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. The view identifies the Decision anchor and its historical reference commit.
2. It renders the historical issue state and later changes as separate evidence.
3. Missing or unavailable bvr/git/transcript sources are explicit and do not erase the rest of the answer.
4. Later reconsideration is shown only when explicitly related.
5. Current and historical views consume the same Provenance model; no migration or second store is introduced.

## Testing
Temporary git/Beads fixtures with custom-status and partial-source failures, plus headless behavioral coverage for historical rendering and unresolved evidence.

description:
Do not resolve this architecture question in passing; confirm the preview trust boundary with the maintainer before implementing it.

Origin: louiselm-d6fv.6.2 (launch preview and Neovim health).

Evidence: skills-core/src/discovery/authentication.rs authenticates input manifests and isolation observations only through an exact signed sequence-zero Launcher receipt. skills-core/src/cli.rs has no preview command. lua/louiselm/health/init.lua does not consume posture, and ordinary Session launch still runs configured Agent commands directly. louiselm-qbr.5.1.2 owns the pending canonical broker Session inspect/status surface. louiselm-d6fv.9 remains the only consumer allowed to enable user-visible Verified launch.

Decision needed: should .6.2 build an artifact-based prospective preflight now, clearly distinguishing proposed identities and unproven controls from authenticated historical evidence, or should preview read through a broker-owned authoritative prelaunch/status endpoint first? These require different input contracts and ownership; do not invent a parallel authority store or treat an old successful receipt as proof of a future or currently running Session.

title: Withdraw historical usage batches and reimport corrections
description:
## Goal
Correct a mistaken historical declaration by withdrawing its batch from analytics and importing a corrected batch without erasing evidence.
## Scope
Explicit withdrawal, audit retention, active-batch queries and corrected reimport. No mutation/deletion of live facts or original imported declarations.
## Acceptance
A named batch can be explicitly withdrawn idempotently, with actor/time/reference recorded. Default statistics, picker, attribution filters and imported replay consumers exclude withdrawn contributions; original rows/declaration remain inspectable as withdrawn. Corrected attribution uses a new confirmed import and is counted once. Duplicate active source evidence still conflicts; withdrawal neither hides live observations nor permits conflicting live-record replacement. Failed withdrawal is atomic and safely retryable. Expose explicit operator/API path, not automatic cleanup. Docs explain retained audit and corrected reimport.
## Testing
Import -> query -> withdraw -> query -> corrected reimport; repeated withdrawal, live overlap, failed write rollback/recovery, attribution filters, visible audit retention and no duplicate counts. Full Lua gates.
## Notes
louiselm-b1uo/4lh8 confirmed contract. Depend on confirmed batch import; preserve immutable fact discipline using separate withdrawal state/events. No guessed corrections.

title: Grill-me needed: which Session processes may use the Agent capability channel directly?
description:
Do not resolve this question in passing; use a focused grill-me session.

qbr.5.1.1 acceptance 6 requires top-level Agent host-PID binding, denies children direct authority, and treats deliberate parent proxying as the Agent effect. The prerequisite implementation instead binds assigned UID/GID plus Session process-tree membership. Which policy must the Control broker enforce, and what trusted evidence identifies its authorized process?

Evidence: d6fv.4.4 comments 698/713 observed Bubblewrap 0.12 child-pid as the namespace PID1 reaper, with the Agent shell beneath it; they direct capability authentication through assigned UID and cgroup membership/descendance. skills-core/src/launch_supervisor.rs:154-157 explicitly says sandbox_leader_pid is not the Agent packet identity. skills-core/src/launch_supervisor/system.rs:1046-1064 accepts any matching Session member; :1213-1219 pins only UID/GID. It retains the connection but has no capability request consumer yet. skills-core/src/launch_transport.rs:97-115 distinguishes process pins from identity pins. No actual Agent/workload host PID is exposed by the current sandbox API.

Threads: parent-only direct authority versus whole-Session authority; wrappers and Agent subprocesses; proving the actual workload host PID without treating the reaper or an Agent claim as identity; PID reuse and per-message credentials; child denial and deliberate parent proxying; whether launcher authentication must change or broker supplies the additional restriction. Preserve Bubblewrap reaping/lifecycle behavior; --as-pid-1 was previously rejected. Resolve the task and prerequisite record together before implementing this authority boundary.

Found while implementing qbr.5.1.1 in codex/01a083f4-469e-7351-97fb-205f6aa39a6f. No runtime changes made.
design: Maintainer confirmed the final shared-understanding summary on 2026-09-09 in codex/01a083f4-469e-7351-97fb-205f6aa39a6f. Exactly one supervisor-authenticated actual Agent runtime holds full authority. Tools/helpers require explicit narrower grants; automatic delegation needs pre-existing operator permission. Kernel-backed identity/lifetime proof and enforced Agent/tool separation are mandatory; membership, reaper PID, self-claim and first connection are insufficient. Agent-originated proxy requests remain Agent effects under its permissions/approvals/audit, without prompt-injection immunity. Agent exit revokes all delegated authority; replacement requires fresh launch. Seq0 durable ACK -> restricted initialization without effects -> verify identity and tool isolation -> enable capabilities -> seq1 Running durable ACK -> success. Failure ends launch. Unsupported ordinary Sessions may remain available without claiming protection. No runtime wrapper or altered Bubblewrap reaping authorized.

No runtime code changed; concrete identity/isolation mechanisms still need implementation proof within the confirmed constraints.

title: Reflect on Yegge's rewrite-and-delete guidance for louiselm
description:
## Question

After reading Julien Danjou's commentary, what should louiselm deliberately adopt or reject from Steve Yegge's advice about deleting tests/code and rebuilding systems for agents?

## Source

- Julien Danjou: https://julien.danjou.info/blog/steve-yegge-deleted-the-wrong-thing/
- Steve Yegge's primary essay: https://www.yegge.ai/essays/six-new-tips-for-better-coding-with-agents/

## Findings to check

Yegge argues that, in an agent-assisted workflow, generating a replacement can be easier than repairing a heavily changed system. He describes deleting and regenerating tests after a large refactor because the agent could target the new behavior more directly, and generalizes that code may be cheaper to throw away and recreate than to preserve indefinitely. The counter-risk is reward hacking: an agent can make tests green by deleting or weakening the oracle, while the project loses knowledge encoded in the old tests.

Read Danjou's framing closely and decide whether the title's “wrong thing” is the code, the tests, or the surrounding engineering assumptions. Record where his argument agrees or disagrees with Yegge rather than treating either as a blanket rule.

## Initial louiselm reflection

- louiselm is small, early-stage, and explicitly permits breaking changes, so focused rewrites may be rational when a boundary or model is genuinely wrong.
- The project's tests are not just implementation ballast: they encode public APIs, ACP protocol validation, lifecycle/disposal behavior, fast-event scheduling boundaries, and security invariants. Deleting them would remove exactly the durable context agents need.
- A safe “delete and recreate” move should therefore require an explicit replacement contract: identify the obsolete behavior, preserve tests for unchanged contracts, add tests for the new behavior, and show that the suite still exercises failure and lifecycle paths.
- Beads and AGENTS.md should be treated as part of the project's memory. If a rule or failure mode matters, record it before removing the code or test that currently demonstrates it.
- Review granularity matters more as agents produce more code. Prefer small, coherent commits and public-behavior tests that let a human review the intended change without rereading the whole repository.

## Desired outcome

A short design note or follow-up beads answering:

1. When is deleting/regenerating a louiselm test suite justified?
2. Which test categories are non-disposable (protocol, security, lifecycle, async/UI boundary)?
3. What evidence prevents an agent from gaming the green check by deleting coverage?
4. Should the contributor workflow add an explicit “replacement tests and preserved contracts” checklist?

## Out of scope

Do not delete tests, rewrite production code, or add workflow machinery as part of this reading exercise. Create implementation beads only if the reflection identifies a concrete gap.
close_reason: Recorded a contract-first replacement policy in AGENTS.md: regeneration requires intentional behavior change, unchanged protocol/security/lifecycle/async/UI/error coverage must survive, and green status alone is insufficient evidence.

comments.author: codex/01a02fdb-a153-7832-9330-6b3fefe34864
comments.text: Decision: adopt focused code or test replacement when a recorded behavior contract intentionally changes and regeneration is clearer than incremental repair; reject blanket deletion based on age, refactor size, or agent convenience. Yegge’s 2025 essay supplies the delete-and-regenerate-test example and also concedes that years of accumulated nuance may be uneconomical to recreate. Danjou’s 2026 “wrong thing” is not a direct rebuttal of that test example: it addresses Yegge’s later Land Rush workflow and argues that bulk landing deletes the mapping from a failure to its owner, goal, and plan. Applied here, the common constraint is to preserve intent and executable oracles across replacement. AGENTS.md now requires an explicit replacement contract, preservation or porting of unchanged public/API, protocol, security, lifecycle/disposal, async/fast-event, UI-boundary, and error-path coverage, plus evidence that replacement tests detect wrong behavior where practical. A green check or test count alone is insufficient. No follow-up implementation bead is needed because this documentation change closes the concrete workflow gap.

title: Resumed reasoning blocks lose their folds
description:
A resumed Session renders replayed reasoning text and `[thinking]` headers, but its historical reasoning paragraphs are not actual Neovim folds. Reasoning produced after resume folds normally, so one buffer presents identical-looking reasoning blocks with different behavior.

## Observed

Confirmed live on 2026-08-28 in resumed Session `codex/01a04635-f2b8-7e70-9485-7a931923ec99`, buffer 17. The Session header reports `source=loaded`.

Live-instance introspection through `$NVIM` found:

```text
view.thought_folds: 28 recorded ranges
view.thought_fold_counts[1000]: 28
replayed [thinking] headers at lines 175..318: foldlevel=0, foldclosed=-1
post-resume [thinking] headers from line 331 onward: foldlevel=1, closed folds
```

The first replayed range is recorded as zero-based `{ first = 174, last = 175 }`, yet line 175 has no fold. A post-resume range `{ first = 330, last = 335 }` is a real closed fold at lines 331-336. This proves the Agent replayed the reasoning content and LouiseLM recorded the intended ranges; the failure is in the UI fold lifecycle, not missing ACP history.

## Symptoms

- Historical `[thinking]` blocks in a resumed Session cannot be toggled with `za` because no fold exists.
- New `[thinking]` blocks in that same view are closed folds and toggle normally.
- Internal counters claim all reasoning folds were applied, hiding the divergence from later refreshes.

## Root cause

`lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua:1129-1142` installs each manual fold incrementally and advances `view.thought_fold_counts[win]`. During `session/load` replay, later transcript buffer edits invalidate earlier Neovim manual folds, but the count remains at the number of recorded ranges. At replay completion, `handle_event` closes only the trailing run (`init.lua:2172-2179`) and does not rebuild prior folds, so `apply_thought_folds` considers them already applied.

## Why it was not caught

`tests/session/api_spec.lua` proves replayed `agent_thought_chunk` notifications become `thought_chunk` events, while the chat resume coverage in `tests/ui/chat_spec.lua` checks replayed prose and Session attachment. No UI test drives multiple replayed reasoning paragraphs through the ready boundary and then inspects the resulting fold ranges.

## Fix direction

At the replay completion boundary, rebuild reasoning folds for the active window from `view.thought_folds` instead of trusting the incremental count accumulated while the buffer was still changing. Keep the repair at the fold-application boundary; do not persist fold state in ACP or duplicate reasoning content.

## Acceptance

- A chat-level regression emits replayed thought chunks separated by prose/tool boundaries, completes `session/load`, and proves every historical `[thinking]` paragraph has the expected manual fold.
- Reasoning emitted after resume continues to create and toggle folds normally.
- In the live reproduction, historical and post-resume `[thinking]` headers have equivalent fold behavior.

## Not covered

- Preserving whether the user manually opened or closed an individual fold across editor exit; this report concerns reconstructing the fold structure, not persisting per-window open/closed UI state.
- Other manual fold types such as submitted context and completed tool runs were not inspected for the same replay invalidation pattern.
close_reason: Fixed in c1b293d. Current isolated fold-rebuild regression passes, and the maintainer confirmed live that a resumed historical [thinking] fold toggles with za; louiselm-p0kz records the earlier independent live pass.

Regardless of the exact external mechanism, the class of defect is real and testable: something

passes with the fix. Full suite (724 cases) and `stylua --check .` clean.

Per the issue's own "Not covered" section, `apply_context_folds` and `apply_tool_folds` share
the identical incremental-counter shape and were not touched -- this fix is scoped to reasoning
folds only, matching what was filed and reproduced.

title: Retired signing keys still verify new approvals
description:
Retired primary keys can verify newly signed Generation payloads, contrary to retirement's history-only contract. This blocks safe paper recovery (.11.2 AC4).

## Observed
codex/01a07753-51de-7733-bfeb-8a3f26fa907e, 2026-09-06. RED: cargo test --locked --test admission retired_keys_verify_only_admissions_recorded_before_retirement -- --exact: 1 failed, assertion "a retired key must not authorize a new payload, even when backdated". Test creates an Admission, rotates the primary, changes its payload, signs after retirement with the old key and backdates the unsigned admitted_at_ms field; verify_record returns Ok. Real software-key signatures; no hardware/live incident claimed.

## Root cause
admission.rs:302 accepts any valid signature from TrustStore::admission_verification_keys (trust.rs:262), which includes every retired primary without an approved-subject bound. admit loads trust before signing without sharing rotation's lock, permitting an in-flight stale signer to publish after retirement.

## Fix
Record exact successfully authorized subject digests at the protected trust boundary. Serialize approval registration and key retirement; permit retired keys to verify only registered history. Do not use signer-supplied timestamps as retirement evidence.

## Acceptance
Preserve pre-retirement approvals, reject new/backdated payloads and wrong-role signatures from retired keys, cover signing racing with retirement and failed registration. Keep release history equally digest-bound when adding its record. Full skills-core gates.

## Boundaries
Trusted store owner/kernel remain trusted. This demonstrates the public verifier defect, not an unprivileged write into a root-owned installed store.
close_reason: gate:skills-core/tests/admission.rs — registered history survives retirement; new/backdated signatures, concurrent retirement and failed registration refuse. Release history equally bound. Rust gates pass; lessons in prior comment.

Admission and release signing now hold the trust lock through signing and durable registration (admission.rs:187, release.rs:424). verification_keys at trust.rs:308 admits retired keys only for registered subjects. RED backdated fresh signature accepted; GREEN history/new-payload, in-flight signer vs retirement, and failed-registration preservation regressions. A failed registration can leave a pending record but cannot become retired-key history. Full Rust gates pass; no installed/root exploit claim or new design question.

title: Measure usage queries before choosing another execution host
description:
## Goal

Decide whether an owned Rust query host would solve a demonstrated problem in the working usage tools.

## Scope

In: reproducible measurements of SQL execution, sqlite3 process overhead, result transfer, and Lua rendering with representative queries/data. Out: implementing a speculative Rust binary or changing retention to hide slow queries.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Measure the real picker and explorer query paths at current history size and documented grown-history fixtures that preserve representative dimension cardinality and sparse telemetry.
2. Separate cold/warm database time, process overhead, and UI rendering; record environment, dataset shape, commands, and repeated-run results.
3. Preserve exact cohort/coverage results while comparing alternatives. Correctness is not traded for a faster misleading answer.
4. Record an evidence-backed recommendation: keep SQL/Lua, tune a demonstrated bottleneck, or scope an owned Rust query host for measured overhead or a concrete independent consumer.
5. File any justified implementation follow-up with its evidence before closing. SQL aggregate semantics remain canonical; an additional host does not imply rewriting calculations in Rust.

## Testing

Use existing toolchain facilities and deterministic nonsensitive fixtures; no new benchmark dependency. Keep a reproducible check if custom measurement code is needed and record results in the issue. Do not call an unrun benchmark a performance finding.

## Notes

Baseline observed 2026-09-07: old JSON usage store 413155 bytes and 1994 exact rows; this does not prove the new design is fast or that Rust is needed. Source: maintainer's explicit calculation-host question and decision 14 in louiselm-3x9p.
close_reason: gate:docs/performance/usage-20260924/benchmark.py reproducible equality-checked current/1x/10x/100x measurements support SQL/Lua; broad SQL tuning filed as louiselm-sawgo; report and raw repetitions retained
