title: Compare CodeCompanion ACP Grok behavior with LouiseLM
description:
Investigate https://github.com/olimorris/codecompanion.nvim/pull/3357/changes and compare its ACP Grok implementation with LouiseLM. The goal is to identify protocol, context, capability, metadata, lifecycle, or UX differences that could explain behavior we cannot reliably test because the maintainer currently has only rare free Grok API calls.

Focus especially on the `_x.ai/ask_user_question` fields and related `_x.ai/*` values: determine whether they are ACP protocol fields, vendor metadata, request/response extensions, or presentation artifacts; trace how CodeCompanion receives, validates, routes, and renders them; and compare the corresponding LouiseLM paths. Also revisit the earlier x_search investigation: establish whether the implementation/context differences help explain Grok broadening a narrow x_search request into skills/repository/web fallback work and exhausting free quota (see louiselm-bvo5).

Use prior beads as context: louiselm-yyvx (Grok `_meta.x.ai/sessionConfig.options` is not standard configOptions), louiselm-bvo5 (x_search quota exhaustion and unexplained task expansion), and louiselm-tw9d (post-success Grok process exit). Search closed beads with `-a` for additional related evidence before implementation.

Deliverables:
- A concise comparison of the two implementations with file/line or upstream-link evidence.
- A classification of each relevant `_x.ai` field and whether LouiseLM should understand, preserve, ignore, or surface it.
- A concrete recommendation for follow-up code, diagnostics, fixtures, or live-test strategy, separated from hypotheses that require a real Grok run.
- If a new defect or design question is found, file it as a separate bead before changing code.

No code change is implied by this investigation task; do not add Grok-specific compatibility behavior until the evidence supports it.
close_reason: Comparison recorded with upstream source evidence; follow-ups louiselm-01qt and louiselm-byvq. inert:louiselm-byvq

comments.author: codex/01a0666c-476c-7d82-8137-f9b038e295a6
comments.text:
Comparison at upstream heads inspected 2026-09-03: CodeCompanion PR #3357 commit edb43f1bb5852c9e38204e6455973b15c151a1a3; Grok Build commit 72a61251fcffb464bcc687aeb5a998e5a98ec0c9.

Field classification:
- `_x.ai/ask_user_question` and `_x.ai/exit_plan_mode`: top-level JSON-RPC method names produced by ACP ExtRequest wrapping, not `_meta`. The canonical inner methods are `x.ai/ask_user_question` and `x.ai/exit_plan_mode`; wrapped requests nest `{ method, params }` under top-level params. Grok source: https://github.com/xai-org/grok-build/blob/72a61251fcffb464bcc687aeb5a998e5a98ec0c9/crates/codegen/xai-grok-shell/src/leader/server.rs#L446-L455 and https://github.com/xai-org/grok-build/blob/72a61251fcffb464bcc687aeb5a998e5a98ec0c9/crates/codegen/xai-grok-shell/src/session/acp_session_impl/spawn.rs#L2086-L2155.
- Question request fields `sessionId`, `toolCallId`, `questions`, `mode`; question fields `question`, `options`, `multiSelect`; option fields `label`, `description`, `preview`: vendor extension payload, to validate and consume only inside Grok support. Response fields are `outcome`, ordered `answers`, optional `annotations.{question}.{preview,notes}`. Official types: https://github.com/xai-org/grok-build/blob/72a61251fcffb464bcc687aeb5a998e5a98ec0c9/crates/codegen/xai-grok-tools/src/implementations/grok_build/ask_user_question/types.rs.
- Plan request fields `sessionId`, `toolCallId`, `planContent`; response `outcome` plus optional `feedback`: same vendor extension classification. Official types: https://github.com/xai-org/grok-build/blob/72a61251fcffb464bcc687aeb5a998e5a98ec0c9/crates/codegen/xai-grok-tools/src/implementations/grok_build/exit_plan_mode/types.rs.
- `_meta.x.ai/sessionConfig.options`: actual ACP metadata namespace, distinct from the methods above; prior disposition remains louiselm-yyvx.

Implementation comparison:
- Both launch `grok agent stdio` and speak ACP v1.
- CodeCompanion adds an adapter-scoped reverse-request handler, direct/wrapped normalization, question/plan UI, exact response mapping, exactly-once guards, and cleanup on completion/error/cancel/process exit: https://github.com/olimorris/codecompanion.nvim/blob/edb43f1bb5852c9e38204e6455973b15c151a1a3/lua/codecompanion/adapters/acp/grok.lua and https://github.com/olimorris/codecompanion.nvim/blob/edb43f1bb5852c9e38204e6455973b15c151a1a3/lua/codecompanion/acp/init.lua#L691-L815.
- LouiseLM routes every reverse request into Session, but handles only `session/request_permission`; unsupported requests return without any response (`lua/louiselm/session/lifecycle.lua:507-510`). That is worse than merely lacking Grok UI because Grok documents these as blocking requests whose tool loop waits on the reply. Filed generic bug louiselm-01qt.
- LouiseLM has no typed question/plan event or pending-interaction lifecycle. Filed capability feature louiselm-byvq. Its implementation should preserve the core/UI boundary and not copy CodeCompanion’s adapter callback structure blindly.
- CodeCompanion advertises ACP fs read/write while LouiseLM explicitly advertises false. This is a deliberate client capability difference, not evidence about Grok x_search behavior.
- Prompt behavior is materially similar at the relevant level: CodeCompanion sends only unsent user messages; LouiseLM sends the new turn plus explicitly staged context. PR #3357 changes prompt code only to cancel pending extension requests.

`x_search` conclusion: PR #3357 contains no x_search handler, quota logic, model-call cap, fallback policy, or prompt instruction. It gives no evidence that the reverse-request gap caused louiselm-bvo5’s broad skills/repository/web expansion. Keep bvo5’s controlled minimal-context reproduction and rate-limit diagnosis separate. The difference in fs capability and LouiseLM’s attached AGENTS.md context are hypotheses only and require a real bounded run.

Upstream caution: PR review https://github.com/olimorris/codecompanion.nvim/pull/3357#discussion_r3921942074 identifies an active-input cancellation hole in plan feedback. LouiseLM’s follow-up explicitly requires cancellation across every terminal path and late-callback suppression.

Recommendation: land louiselm-01qt first as the small protocol-safe fallback. Treat louiselm-byvq as separate provider-specific capability work with official-source fixtures and eventual live acceptance; spend no Grok quota on x_search until deterministic fixtures and a one-call bounded script exist.

Lesson route: issue-local comparison is this comment; actionable work is louiselm-01qt and louiselm-byvq; no AGENTS.md convention or needs-design question is warranted.

title: QA round: current HEAD cd66b47
description:
# Manual QA review — current HEAD after the Aug 28 broad UI round

Working file for the current round. You run the steps, I edit this file as we
learn. Untracked on purpose; tell me to commit or delete it when we are done.

**Build under test:** `ded81aa..cd66b47` (current HEAD, 2026-08-31). Re-run
Setup after any fix.

Origin: the last completed broad UI round predates the current HEAD. Since
then, Session timeout and permission lifecycle fixes, chat navigation,
workflow/Run changes, Provenance changes, and the Android receiver-migration
fix landed. The older `p0kz`, `klm2`, and `1orv` rounds also left cases blocked
or unverified; this round closes those evidence gaps where their prerequisites
are now fixed.

## Status

| # | Case | State |
|---|------|-------|
| 1 | Real ACP turn with tool permission and completion | passed (`769df194…`) |
| 2 | Chat navigation and prompt return on current HEAD | passed (`769df194…`) |
| 3 | Provenance Decision timeline and loading state | passed (`769df194…`); latency filed in `louiselm-cvlc` |
| 4 | Cold Park/resume restores claims and Run budget | partial; durable resume bug `louiselm-brp7` |
| 5 | Handoff retains the source Session | passed (`3a60a5b4…` → `b5972129…`) |
| 6 | Receiver migration starts uploads without manual Sync | passed (`8de99c6b…`) |

## Setup

From the repository root:

```sh
git rev-parse --short HEAD
git diff --check
```

The first command must print `cd66b47`. Start a fresh Neovim from this checkout
with an isolated state directory so remembered permissions from another review
cannot affect Case 1:

```sh
QA_STATE=$(mktemp -d /tmp/louiselm-qa-state.XXXXXX)
XDG_STATE_HOME="$QA_STATE" nvim -u ./manual_init.lua
```

Alternatively, in an existing instance run `:LouiselmPermissions` and revoke
the matching `allow always` rules before starting the case. Restart it after
any Lua change. Use a real ACP Agent in its normal permission mode for Case 1
and Case 4. Do not use a skip-approval or yolo mode: it makes permission cases
untestable. Do not Park
the Session driving this review; use a disposable second Session.

Cases 3–5 are UI/manual gaps only. The automated suite already covers the
typed event, transcript, workflow, and transport contracts. Do not repeat
those tests as manual evidence.

For Case 4, build the current capture service and put it first in the PATH
before starting Neovim:

```sh
cargo build --release --manifest-path capture-service/Cargo.toml
PATH="$PWD/capture-service/target/release:$PATH" nvim -u ./manual_init.lua
```

Confirm inside Neovim with `:lua print(vim.fn.exepath("louiselm-capture"))`.
Use `:LouiselmSessionId` to identify the disposable Session. If Case 4 uses a
Beads claim, save its prior status and assignee and restore them in Cleanup.

## Ground rules learned the hard way

- The old Park round used a shell-created Run and therefore did not prove the
  production `Run:park_cold` path. A valid Case 4 must use the normal LouiseLM
  Park command from a live Session with `loadSession` advertised.
- Restart after changing PATH or the live Neovim may keep resolving the stale
  installed capture binary. Verify `exepath` before the Park case.
- Pin ACP evidence by the Session id returned by `:LouiselmSessionId`; never
  inspect whichever log directory happens to be newest.
- The live instance used for the first attempt had 20 persistent `always`
  rules. Clear that state or use the isolated state setup above; do not infer
  a product failure from a bypassed request.
- A read-only Agent tool may be auto-approved and does not exercise LouiseLM's
  permission gate. Use a unique disposable file edit for this case.

## Cases

### 1. Real ACP turn with tool permission and completion

Exercises `27cba00`, `7400f10`, `c5a7046`, `c36487f`, and `23c56bf` through the
live Agent boundary.

Steps:

> Start a fresh real Session in normal permission mode. Substitute a unique
> suffix for `STAMP`, then ask: “Create the disposable file
> `/tmp/louiselm-qa-permission-STAMP.txt` containing exactly `qa marker`; do
> not modify the repository or perform any other operation.” When the
> permission prompt appears, allow the file edit once. After the answer
> completes, send one ordinary follow-up prompt, then remove the disposable
> file.

Expect: a LouiseLM permission prompt is visible and actionable before the edit;
the tool row and answer appear in order; the Session returns to `ready` after
each turn; the follow-up starts normally. If thinking is emitted, it appears
as a collapsed `[thinking]` block rather than answer prose.

Failure signature: no permission prompt appears for the unique file edit, the
Session remains prompting after the final permission, reports ready before a
queued permission is answered, dies during a normal turn, or the follow-up
cannot start. If the unique file edit still bypasses permission, stop: that is
an Agent permission-mode/configuration problem, not evidence about LouiseLM.

Evidence: report the Session id and inspect its pinned ACP log for
`session/request_permission`, the ordered `session/update` kinds, and the
terminal prompt response. This proves protocol ordering and completion; the
visible permission interaction still rests on the keyboard observation.

First-attempt note: Session `788da2ba-15d3-4a29-8a3d-119a74c03c8a` produced a
tool call and `stopReason=end_turn` but no `session/request_permission`; it used
the read-only prompt above, so this was a recipe miss rather than a product
finding.

Observed pass: Session `769df194-9e9c-4604-8370-3f0b2bde9c53` in isolated state
recorded two prompts, one `session/request_permission` for an `execute` tool,
one `allow` response, a completed tool update, and `end_turn` for both the
permission turn and the ordinary follow-up. The keyboard observation confirmed
the permission prompt and normal ready state.

### 2. Chat navigation and prompt return on current HEAD

Exercises `5d21d90` and the buffer-local navigation in
`lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua`.

Steps:

> In a fresh chat, complete at least two prompts, including one response with
> a folded thinking block or tool row. Press `<Esc>` to Normal mode, then use
> `]u` / `[u` and `]r` / `[r`, including a count such as `2]u`. Place the cursor
> on a transcript row and press `<CR>`.

Expect: each motion lands on the next/previous matching usage or response
boundary, counts are honored, the motions do not unfold or alter content, and
`<CR>` returns to Insert mode on the prompt line at the correct column.

Failure signature: a motion cycles at the buffer edge, lands on the wrong
boundary, changes folds, or `<CR>` inserts into transcript text instead of
returning to the prompt.

Evidence: through the live Neovim socket, inspect the current buffer name,
cursor position, mode, and fold state after each case. This proves routing and
editor state, not just the keymap registration.

Observed pass: In the same Session `769df194-9e9c-4604-8370-3f0b2bde9c53`, the
manual navigation and return-to-prompt interaction worked as expected.

### 3. Provenance Decision timeline and loading state

Exercises the current Provenance path after the older `p0kz` round’s blocked
timeline case became unblocked.

Steps:

> Run the Decision index command (`:LouiselmProvenanceDecisions` or its
> documented mapping), wait for it to load, select a Decision with a closing
> commit, and open its details. Repeat once from a fresh buffer if the view
> already exists.

Expect: a loading view appears immediately; the completed view identifies the
Decision anchor and historical evidence, then presents later backlog changes
as explicit drift rather than rewriting history. Selecting the same Decision
does not raise a duplicate-buffer error.

Failure signature: the UI appears frozen during collection, the historical
and current states are conflated, selection opens the wrong issue, or
`Vim:E95: Buffer with this name already exists` returns.

Evidence: report the `louiselm://` buffer name and capture its final rendered
lines. The buffer text proves the separation and the loading transition; it
does not prove BVR latency outside this selection.

Observed pass: The Provenance view opened correctly twice in the same manual
round. The fetch was visibly slow; this is tracked by the existing open issue
`louiselm-cvlc`.

### 4. Cold Park/resume restores claims and Run budget

Exercises the production Park path after `louiselm-aaw0.1` and
`louiselm-aaw0.1.1` fixed the previous resume blocker.

Steps:

1. In a disposable Session, complete at least one prompt. There is no separate
   user-facing capability toggle: the Park command below checks whether the
   Agent advertised `loadSession`.
2. Claim one low-stakes ready Beads issue to that exact Session id and record
   its prior state/assignee.
3. Run `:LouiselmPark` and confirm the Park action. If it reports `cold Park
   requires an Agent that supports session/load`, stop Case 4 as unavailable
   for this Agent. Do not create the Run only through the capture-service CLI.
4. Close or detach the disposable chat, then run `:LouiselmResumePark` and
   select the new Run.

Expect: Park reports `Session cold-Parked`; resume reports
`cold Park resumed (recoverable, lossy)`; the resumed Session is usable; its
Run owner contains the original claim and the admitted generated-work ceiling.

Failure signature: the picker shows no Run, `session/load` reports a resource
not found for a Session that completed a prompt, claims disappear, the budget
is zeroed, or the resumed chat cannot prompt.

Evidence: save the Run id and inspect `louiselm-capture run list` for the
durable Park, then inspect the resumed Session through the live Neovim socket.
The service record proves persistence; the socket proves the UI-side owner
was restored. Restore the claimed issue during Cleanup.

Observed partial pass: Run `98a5046c-5dd3-4c70-8eda-e7b872f4da72` persisted as
`cold_parked` with `load_session: true` and Session
`claude/769df194-9e9c-4604-8370-3f0b2bde9c53`. The ACP log records three
completed prompts, and the user observed the resumed Session working. However,
the durable record and `louiselm-capture run list` remained `cold_parked` with
`resume_attempt=null` afterward; claim/budget restoration was not independently
verified. Filed as `louiselm-brp7`: `Chat:resume_park` reconstructs only a local
Run and never finalizes the capture-service resume.

### 5. Handoff retains the source Session

Exercises the one unverified case left by `louiselm-1orv`.

Steps:

1. Start a fresh disposable source Session. Do not reuse the resumed Park
   Session from Case 4.
2. Send this prompt and wait for it to finish: “For handoff QA, remember the
   marker BLUE-TEAPOT-42. Reply only `source ready`; do not modify files.”
3. From that source chat, run `:LouiselmHandOff`. LouiseLM creates the target
   Session; choose any different configured Agent in the target picker. Do not
   create the target manually first.
4. In the editable `louiselm://handoff-...` buffer, replace the takeover-task
   placeholder with: “Reply with marker BLUE-TEAPOT-42 and `target ready`; do
   not modify files.” Submit with `<C-s>` from Normal mode.
5. Wait for the target’s first turn to finish. Record its Session id with
   `:LouiselmSessionId`, then run `:LouiselmSessionSwitch` and select the
   original source Session.

Expect: the target receives the reviewed task and compact context, focus lands
on the target while it runs, and the source Session remains listed and
switchable with its prior state intact.

Failure signature: source disappears, source state changes unexpectedly, the
target receives raw tool payloads or no task, or the handoff loops instead of
completing.

Evidence: report source and target Session ids; inspect the target ACP prompt
frame for the ordered text/resource blocks, and confirm the source appears in
the live switcher. The log proves transport shape, while the switcher proves
source retention.

Observed pass: source `claude/3a60a5b4-ea75-4959-af53-705fa54c6124` handed off
to target `claude/b5972129-7947-4751-8175-7ce79823c35d`. Each pinned ACP log has
one prompt and one `end_turn`; the user confirmed the source remains listed and
switchable at will. No product finding.

### 6. Receiver migration starts uploads without manual Sync

Exercises `b618d78`, `MainActivity.kt`, and `UploadWorker.kt` on a real Android
device. This is not covered by the Lua suite or JVM policy test.

Steps:

1. Pair the device with receiver A and create a capture owned by A.
2. Make A unreachable and trigger an upload retry; confirm the capture remains
   pending behind the normal retry delay.
3. Pair receiver B so the app performs a receiver-identity migration. Confirm
   the migration.
4. Keep the device online and wait for the upload worker without pressing
   `Sync now`.

Expect: the migrated capture begins uploading promptly, without waiting for
receiver A’s old retry backoff; the capture UUID, original audio, and queue
ownership remain unchanged.

Failure signature: the capture waits for the old backoff, requires `Sync now`,
duplicates the capture, or is lost during ownership migration.

Evidence: record the capture UUID, receiver identities, and WorkManager state
from `adb shell dumpsys jobscheduler` or WorkManager diagnostics; confirm one
receiver-B copy and one uploaded marker. Do not include credentials, QR
payloads, audio, or request bodies in the report.

Observed pass: with receiver A stopped, the phone migrated one pending capture
to temporary receiver B and its pending count changed from 1 to 0 without
pressing **Sync now**. B reports one capture, UUID
`8de99c6b-76aa-4dd5-80ab-98d09eaebb6a`, and one paired device. Receiver A was
stopped for the test and must be started again during cleanup. No product
finding.

## Evidence check

Pin every Session, Run, capture UUID, and buffer name in the report. A green
headless suite is not evidence for focus, modal behavior, real ACP event order,
or Android WorkManager backoff replacement.

## Cleanup when the round closes

- Restore the claimed Beads issue to its exact prior state and assignee.
- Dispose disposable Sessions and close extra Neovim windows.
- Remove temporary Run records or let their declared TTL expire.
- Remove temporary Android captures and test receiver state only after their
  UUIDs and outcomes are recorded.
- Delete this scratch file only after its final content becomes the round bead.

## Reporting back

Send me the case number, what you saw, the Session/Run/capture id, and any
surprising detail. I pull objective evidence before classifying a finding.

## Findings this round

- `louiselm-brp7` — Cold Park resume leaves the durable Run `cold_parked`;
  filed from Case 4 evidence.
close_reason: Round complete: Cases 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6 passed; Case 4 exposed louiselm-brp7. Durable report captured in this issue; scratch deleted after sync.

title: Design Flotsam: standalone recovery from the ACP log-loss incident
description:
## Problem Statement

Use the 2026-09-09 accidental deletion of ~/.local/state and the complete ACP-log recovery conversation as the base case for a reusable recovery offering. The maintainer found the outcome useful but the process slow, confusing, stressful and too dependent on ad hoc assistance. They want the lessons retained and investigated, not another identical scan. The product must be SEPARATE FROM LOUISELM. This tracker records the proposal until a separate home is chosen; it is not a LouiseLM feature, crate, plugin or dependency.

## Proposed Outcome / Current Authority

A focused discovery epic producing an evidence-backed postmortem, threat model, performance study plan, and a small approved MVP proposal. Compare a skill/runbook using existing utilities, a minimal standalone CLI with optional skill guidance, and a larger product. Rust is a candidate only: do not commit to a rewrite, implementation architecture, schedule or commercial product before measuring the actual gaps and cost. The maintainer requested P0 and explicitly expressed uncertainty about scope and effort.

## User Stories

1. As someone who just deleted valuable files, I want immediate preservation guidance and an honest assessment of what can still be attempted.
2. With one or two small USB keys and no full-image-sized spare drive, I want an explicit evidence/space tradeoff and preservation of unrelated destination files.
3. I want reliable boot preparation and short phone-readable instructions that work without Neovim, the original OS, networking or an active assistant.
4. I want visible progress, safe cancellation/resumption and an explanation of what another pass could add.
5. I want intact files, historical snapshots, complete records, unscoped data and partial fragments distinguished, with traceable byte origins and no invented completeness.
6. I want root access limited to the necessary acquisition operations and recovered content treated as untrusted data, even when an AI assistant coordinates the workflow.

## Lessons and Design Questions to Carry Forward

- Preservation first: identify source and destination, active writes/swap/discard risk and offline feasibility early. Separate emergency live salvage from offline acquisition and analysis of saved evidence. State clearly when continued normal use can reduce remaining options; do not imply that protection applied later restores an earlier point in time.
- Device identity: letters changed across boots in this case. Bind operations to serial/UUID/size/partition geometry, revalidate actual opened objects and mount destinations, reject ambiguous or substituted devices. Never use a guessed /dev/sdX identity.
- Constrained storage: make full-image availability explicit; if unavailable, choose a bounded acquisition plan, preserve raw metadata and selected bytes, document omissions and leave space for final reports. Do not equate targeted capture with a full image. Preserve existing USB data unless exact overwrites are separately authorized.
- Offline UX: the original Debian installer boot failed/froze, then a compatible custom RAM environment succeeded. Account for firmware mode, virtual USB CD versus USB HDD, storage/input drivers and machine compatibility. Provide authenticated/pinned assets, preflight checks and clear independent operator instructions. Do not require rebuilding an initramfs interactively for every user.
- Workflow: inventory/preservation -> metadata/journal analysis -> planned extraction/content carving -> evidence reconciliation -> optional restoration. Keep analysis reusable over captured bytes; avoid repeating a completed search without a stated new hypothesis. Checkpoint phase, coverage, identities, space and remaining hypotheses durably before reboot/handoff.
- Evidence: preserve exact raw spans, offsets, hashes, acquisition metadata, parser/baseline versions, coverage, exclusions and stop reasons. Distinguish scan completion, raw-byte capture, recognized records, duplicate records, new records and file completeness. Keep originals immutable and partial/unscoped/ambiguous reconstructions separate; preview restoration and handle collisions without blind append/overwrite.
- Performance: measure end-to-end recovery time separately from read/parse/hash/dedup/write/readback phases, memory use and boot/operator time. The final targeted scan's report records approximately 63.5 seconds for 308,893,975 raw bytes; this is not an isolated language benchmark, sustained device-throughput claim, or evidence Python caused the day-long process. Compare implementations on the same immutable fixture with correctness and safety parity before claiming a Rust speedup. Investigate algorithm/I/O and workflow improvements first; retain readback verification unless equivalent integrity is demonstrated.
- Privilege/security: broad sudo grants amplify both mistakes and compromise. This is a potential attack surface, NOT evidence an attack happened today. Evaluate a narrowly scoped, auditable acquisition helper and unprivileged parsers/analysis, fixed verified operation plans, minimal inherited environment/FDs, no unrelated access/network by default and explicit disclosure boundaries. Treat recovered log text, filenames, filesystem metadata, manifests and web instructions as untrusted input, never executable instructions or authorization. Cover prompt/shell injection, malformed inputs/resource exhaustion, symlink/path traversal, device/destination substitution, credential exposure and rescue-component supply authenticity. A skill alone is not a privilege boundary; kernel read-only flags are not a hardware write blocker. Do not make global repetitive approval prompts a substitute for bounded authority.
- Destination health: the photos show a FAT unclean-unmount warning on the output USB. The saved outputs subsequently passed independent size/hash and parser replay checks. Preserve both facts; neither a warning alone proves corruption nor passing file hashes proves the whole volume healthy. Define dirty-destination/repair policy without automatically running fsck on original evidence.

## Discovery Acceptance Criteria

1. Preserve a self-contained incident timeline, outcome ledger, successful/failed approaches and artifact index in this issue's evidence; no requirement to reopen the entire chat to understand the case. Do not publish raw transcripts or turn private recovered data into public fixtures.
2. Produce a threat model covering privileged acquisition, untrusted media/content, agent instructions, output integrity and optional restoration, with concrete enforceable boundaries and residual risks.
3. Compare skill/runbook, thin standalone tool and larger product against this case; recommend the smallest useful option with an effort range and explicit uncertainty. Confirm an external project home with the maintainer before any implementation there; do not initialize it now.
4. Specify a reproducible performance/correctness comparison using synthetic or explicitly approved private fixtures. A language decision must cite measured bottlenecks, portability/deployment cost, and equivalent recovery results and safeguards.
5. Propose a narrowly bounded MVP and acceptance matrix: wrong/swapped source, mounted source or swap, interrupted scan and restart, full/disconnected/dirty destination, malformed/hostile data, duplicate-only findings, uncertain fragments, restoration collisions, compatible boot, durable report, sync/unmount and safe poweroff. Use disposable disk images/VMs, never destructive tests against the incident SSD.
6. Review the proposal with the maintainer before creating implementation slices. Completion here means an approved evidence-backed scope and plan, not a finished recovery engine. Keep further recovery of today's logs separate and explicitly authorized.

## Out of Scope

LouiseLM implementation; changing its canonical Forensics or Provenance meanings; copying its signing/passkey recovery feature; a universal filesystem recovery promise; guaranteed full recovery of the historical 951 MB; immediate Rust rewrite; new scans/imports/repairs; new sudo policy; cloud uploads; formatting USBs; purchasing hardware; implementing a skill or launching a business in this filing.

State: standalone-product discovery epic, needs-design, unclaimed. Detailed incident evidence and artifact hashes are attached as an issue comment.
notes: Flotsam approved home /home/lotso/code/flotsam; initial main commit e7b152c contains README, guide, sanitized incident, scope, case template, rehearsal, validation and tests. .1 docs and .2 synthetic rehearsal closed; 9 stdlib tests and two command-line trials pass. No production recovery engine or physical-device claim. Name/scope/home/commit authorized by maintainer; no remote configured, destination URL requested for push. Next .3: independent human guide rehearsal; .4: disposable ext4/physical acquisition and hardware acceptance. Keep epic open pending remaining acceptance. Initial tracker remains here. Incident evidence comment1491; approved proposal comment1875; lessons in Flotsam docs/scope.md and docs/validation.md.
close_reason: none:transferred — the whole Flotsam epic family (epic + 4 tasks) now lives at flotsam-design-flotsam-standalone-recovery-zcm in /home/lotso/code/flotsam/.beads, prefix flotsam, initialized 2026-09-17 at the maintainer's request. Descriptions, comments, labels, priorities, closed statuses and blocker edges carried verbatim and verified. Lesson routed: the external-project label was the signal this never belonged in the LouiseLM tracker; a project the contract calls SEPARATE FROM LOUISELM should get its own workspace when it gets its own repo, not a label. No new standing rule warranted.

# Standalone recovery discovery: proposal for review

Issue: louiselm-standalone-recovery-product-ah9s  
Prepared: 2026-09-15  
Status: discovery draft; scope and project home await maintainer decision.

## Recommendation

Start with an offline recovery runbook, a reusable case record, and a synthetic rehearsal. Budget 3–5 focused engineering days for this first deliverable. Use the rehearsal to decide whether a small standalone tool is necessary. A tool becomes justified when a repeated safety check, checkpoint, or result-reconciliation step demonstrably cannot be made dependable with the runbook and existing tools.

The initial audience is a technical Linux operator recovering deleted structured text from a readable ext4 volume, with limited spare storage. This deliberately narrow audience is a proposal, not an approved product commitment. The useful outcome is a repeatable preservation-to-report workflow that another operator can follow without the original chat.

The case does not establish a need for a new recovery engine or a Rust rewrite. The recorded targeted acquisition lasted 63.5 seconds; its surrounding workflow had boot failures, changing device names, constrained storage, multiple handoffs, and confusing distinctions between recovered bytes and intact files. Workflow improvement is the first hypothesis to test.

Everything below is discovery. No new device scan, repair, restore, privilege grant, software implementation, public release, or external project creation has been performed.

## Evidence and confidence

The incident source is Beads comment 1491 on this epic, recorded by the original recovery session. Its complete timeline, private artifact locators, and SHA-256 anchors remain the canonical incident index. This discovery read that record; it did not remount USBs, inspect private log contents, or independently rehash the artifacts. Accordingly, “verified” below describes verification recorded during the incident, not a new verification in this session.

| Phase | Recorded evidence | What it establishes / limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deletion, 9 September | The maintainer reported deletion of `~/.local/state`; ACP logs were the priority. Initial salvage ran on the live mounted system. | The source was changing. Later captures cannot establish its exact state at deletion. |
| Historical inventory | 174 files / 951,348,545 bytes: 143 healthy saved, 6 already identical healthy, 6 damaged, 16 fragmentary, 3 without recovered extent mappings. | These are the recorded inventory categories, not proof that every historical file was complete. |
| Broad salvage | Two passes covered 7,403 candidate groups. The first reached a provenance-output cap. Together they added 244,010 novel records / 249,778,314 bytes beyond an 803,844-record baseline. | Useful new data was recovered. This was not a whole-device point-in-time image. |
| Reconciliation | Combined views held 1,020,620 unique records / 1,246,723,268 bytes, including 7,343 unscoped records. | Views combined overlapping history. Their total is not a percentage of the original 951 MB. |
| Preservation and boot | Two small USB keys held existing data; neither could hold a full source image. Raw evidence included a 1 GiB journal. Debian 12.8 boot attempts failed/froze; a custom RAM environment worked. | Preservation and independent boot were possible, but required case-specific preparation. Recorded prototype tests do not establish broad hardware compatibility. |
| Targeted offline acquisition | 14 unresolved mapped files led to 191 ranges / 308,893,975 bytes in 216 chunks. Recorded audit: source opened read-only, kernel read-only, unmounted, no swap. Elapsed: 63.485417555 seconds. | All planned ranges were captured. Two corroborated snapshots and three unmapped files were outside this plan. Historical extents do not prove current ownership. |
| Replay | Size/hash/coverage checks passed; independent replay matched all 16 parser counters. All 151,477 recognized records were duplicates against a 1,047,854-record baseline. | No new complete records in this pass. Remaining fragments may still be useful; zero novelty does not prove full recovery or impossibility of further recovery. |
| Destination | Photos recorded a FAT unclean-unmount warning. Subsequent saved-file verification passed. | Both facts stand. Neither identifies the warning's cause or certifies the whole filesystem. |

### What worked and what failed

- Worked: retaining raw spans and their origins; preserving existing destination data; carrying checkpoints across reboot; independent hash and parser replay; keeping partial and unscoped results distinct.
- Failed or required intervention: initial boot route; provenance capacity planning; stable device identification across boots; preparation of an independent offline environment; interpreting overlapping outputs and duplicate-only results.
- Unknown: time spent in each phase, exact number of operator interventions, coverage lost before offline preservation, original-file completeness, general hardware compatibility, and language-specific performance.
- Causal interpretation: the destructive deletion was the initiating event. Continued source activity and delayed offline access limited what could be established afterward. The record does not quantify additional loss or prove that discard, overwriting, or an attack caused a particular missing file.

The earlier retention issue, louiselm-proxy-log-evidence-expiry-xxfu comment 648, addressed aggregate log eviction and a one-time backup. The later prevention feature, louiselm-acp-daily-backups-kb31 comment 1515, records maintainer-accepted scheduled encrypted backup and restore. Recovery discovery should not duplicate that completed prevention work.

### Artifact index

All following names are relative to the second USB identified in comment 1491; device letters are intentionally not used here.

- `offline-recovery-20260909/`: instructions, boot assets, source tools, tests, fixed target plan, baseline, VM evidence, and `SHA256SUMS`.
- `acp-offline-results-bu27gn8m/DEVICE-AUDIT.json`: opened-source and environment evidence.
- `acp-offline-results-bu27gn8m/scan/SCAN-REPORT.json`: completion, coverage, counters, and timing.
- `acp-offline-results-bu27gn8m/scan/target-spans.bin` and `target-spans.provenance.jsonl`: saved bytes and physical origins.
- `state-recovery-backup-20260909/RECOVERY/`: earlier raw journal/directory evidence and combined partial views.

Reference anchors from comment 1491: SCAN-REPORT SHA-256 `5322995e85612298cdfd065e1dd37ee5079912c675686f3184a7aeddf258c717`; DEVICE-AUDIT SHA-256 `c2fa6ae34f5807c5fb01ce5b7f5f6704a2fd82a0eb354292efc3b7ce3c713b1f`. Other hashes, device identities, and private photo locators remain in that comment. Public fixtures must be synthetic, not copied from these artifacts.

## Existing tools and the remaining gap

GNU ddrescue already provides acquisition with a mapfile for interruption and resumption, and a domain mapfile can limit which source regions are read. Its manual warns about mounted sources and changing device names. Reuse this capability when the approved destination can hold its output. It does not decide whether a recovered application record is novel or an original file is complete. [GNU ddrescue manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/ddrescue/manual/ddrescue_manual.html)

PhotoRec already provides signature-based carving, partial-file handling, progress, and resumption. It generally does not restore original names or directory structure. Its documentation warns about FAT32 output-size limits. These are reasons to evaluate it for suitable formats, not assume it reconstructs ACP histories. [PhotoRec recovery documentation](https://www.cgsecurity.org/testdisk_doc/photorec.html)

TestDisk and PhotoRec can analyze supported disk-image formats without administrator rights, but do not directly support split raw images. The incident's packed noncontiguous span collection therefore must not be presented as an ordinary complete disk image. [Supported image inputs](https://www.cgsecurity.org/testdisk_doc/running.html)

The unresolved gap is dependable coordination: source/destination binding, realistic storage budgeting, portable checkpoints, bounded record reconciliation, and a report separating coverage from completeness. Whether this needs custom executable code remains an empirical question.

## Options and effort

Estimates are planning judgments for one experienced engineer, including review and rehearsal. They are not measured delivery promises. They assume a readable source, Linux/ext4 scope, synthetic fixtures, and reuse of existing tools. Access to representative hardware and operator review can add calendar delay.

| Option | Deliverable | Effort estimate | Main tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Runbook first — recommended | Phone-readable offline steps, case/checkpoint/report templates, documented supported tool route, one repeatable rehearsal. | 3–5 days, including a 1–2 day feasibility exercise. | Fastest way to test workflow value. Human procedure cannot enforce a privilege boundary. |
| Small standalone tool, if justified | Validate case plans, bind artifacts and checkpoints, budget storage, summarize coverage, and reconcile one structured-record format; optional skill guidance. | 4–8 engineering weeks total for a narrow pilot, including the runbook and hardening. | Machine checks can reduce repeated mistakes; acquisition authority and recovery state add substantial testing obligations. |
| Broader recovery product | Multiple filesystems/formats, general GUI, maintained rescue distribution, installation/support, broader hardware matrix. | At least 3–6 engineer-months as an order-of-magnitude estimate; low confidence. | Boot maintenance, format coverage, packaging, and support dominate; this incident alone does not justify the scope. |

Small-tool estimate basis: 3–5 days workflow/specification; 4–7 days identity/storage/checkpoint handling; 3–6 days bounded record reconciliation; 7–12 days fault injection, privilege review, packaging, and operator rehearsal. These ranges are illustrative, not a schedule or a set of implementation issues. A custom rescue distribution or general filesystem parser would require re-estimation.

## Proposed first milestone

Deliver a runbook and reusable case folder that guide a second technical operator through a synthetic deleted-log incident without the originating assistant. Start with a supported existing rescue environment; list the specific hardware actually exercised. A custom boot distribution is outside this milestone.

The workflow has six stages:

1. Triage: determine whether a usable backup exists; identify source, destination, storage budget, current source activity, and supported environment. If offline preservation is unavailable, clearly record that limitation and stop the supported acquisition route. Emergency live salvage needs its own explicit decision.
2. Preserve: choose a full-image route when space permits. With limited storage, record a bounded plan and its omissions before acquiring anything. If the rehearsal cannot safely support bounded capture using existing facilities, return an unsupported result; this is evidence for a later helper.
3. Checkpoint: retain source/destination identity, exact plan, tool versions, completed coverage, errors, remaining budget, and next hypothesis in a case record that survives reboot.
4. Analyze copies: retain original captures unchanged; perform extraction and reconciliation as an unprivileged user over saved evidence. Restrict the pilot's format claims to the fixture actually tested.
5. Report: separate raw bytes captured, recognized complete records, duplicate records, novel records, fragments, unscoped data, and unknown original-file completeness. Show exclusions and why another pass might help.
6. Finish: verify outputs and report persistence, then verify destination synchronization/unmount before declaring safe removal. Export selected results into a fresh staging directory; original-location restoration is deferred.

Success: two consecutive rehearsals, including one interruption, produce independently verifiable reports; a second operator completes the documented route without undocumented commands; every required refusal in the matrix below is either demonstrated or explicitly unsupported. A useful initial usability target is at most two clarification requests during rehearsal; record the count and revise the guide. This is a proposed target, not incident evidence.

Go/no-go after rehearsal: ship the runbook if it meets these criteria. Propose only the smallest missing helper if a repeatable failure needs enforcement or automation. Do not choose Rust until a measured bottleneck or deployment requirement supports that choice.

## Threat model and proposed boundaries

Assets: original bytes, unrelated destination files, recovery artifacts, private recovered content, and the integrity of completeness/coverage claims. Inputs may include mistaken device choices, hostile filesystem metadata, malformed records, forged manifests, and instructions embedded in recovered text. The original record contains no evidence of an attack.

| Threat | Proposed control / how to verify it | Residual limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wrong device or identity changed after preview | Match stable device identifiers, size, geometry, and actual opened object; reject ambiguity and source/destination overlap. Revalidate when resuming. Test substituted devices and aliases. | Identifiers can be duplicated; a compromised host/kernel can lie. |
| Privileged helper gets broader authority | If built, helper accepts only a bounded read plan and an already selected output location, opens source read-only, and owns no repair/write-to-source operation. Restrict inherited FDs/environment, devices and network through OS confinement. Test denied source writes and unrelated access. | A runbook alone does not enforce this; helper and confinement need separate validation. Root/kernel compromise is outside the claim. |
| Live source changes | Supported acquisition requires offline, unmounted source and no source-backed swap; record verified conditions. Test mount/swap refusal and changes at acquisition boundaries. | Read-only settings do not undo earlier changes or substitute for a hardware write blocker. |
| Recovered content controls the operator or agent | Treat payloads, filenames and manifests as data; escape display controls, bound parsing, and never evaluate content as commands. Analysis has no device privilege, credentials, or network. | Operators can still choose to execute content outside the workflow. |
| Malformed data exhausts resources | Bound record size, nesting, memory, scan budget and output; record rejected spans without losing raw evidence. Test huge/truncated/hostile records. | Bounded rejection can reduce extraction coverage; disclose it. |
| Path escape or destination substitution | Create a fresh case directory; reject links, traversal, collisions and replaced destination objects. Pin the output boundary; never fall back to writing into the mountpoint's underlying filesystem. | Destination media can fail independently. |
| Crash, full destination, or unplug | Reserve room for checkpoints/reports; acknowledge progress only after output and checkpoint durability; validate hashes before resume. Do not report success if the report cannot be persisted. | A lost device may lose all on-device checkpoints; last durable progress is the recovery limit. |
| Forged evidence or changed baseline | Bind plan, captured spans, extraction version, baseline digest and report; keep original bytes immutable and analysis outputs separate. Replay against known fixtures. | Hashes detect changes relative to a trusted anchor; they do not prove original-file completeness or trusted acquisition. |
| Private data leaks or hostile rescue asset | Offline/local processing, synthetic public fixtures, independently authenticated pinned boot/tool assets, and explicitly reviewed exports. | A digest from the same compromised download source is not independent authenticity; the rescue supply chain remains trusted. |
| Restoration overwrites good data | Pilot exports only into fresh staging; report collisions, uncertain attribution and fragments. A later restore operation requires preview and explicit destination choice. | The pilot does not restore original paths automatically. |

Dirty-destination policy: prefer a separate known-clean destination. If the only destination is dirty or fails checks, stop the supported route and preserve its existing data; filesystem repair is a separate operation, never an automatic “fix.” Passing artifact hashes does not clear a filesystem-health warning.

## Acceptance matrix for a future pilot

These are proposed tests, not executed tests. Use disposable images and VMs. Physical boot tests require agreed disposable media; the incident SSD is never a test target.

| Scenario | Required observable result |
| --- | --- |
| Wrong/swapped source, changed geometry, duplicate IDs | Refusal before capture; no source writes and no destination overwrite. |
| Source and destination alias or share the endangered source device | Refusal with a precise overlap explanation. |
| Mounted source, active source-backed swap, or unavailable offline mode | Supported acquisition does not start; limitation is durable. |
| Limited space, FAT32-sized output constraint, existing USB files | Plan fits bounded output plus checkpoint reserve; omitted coverage is visible; existing files remain byte-identical. Unsupported output layout is rejected. |
| Cancellation or crash between chunk and checkpoint | Resume validates the plan and completed bytes; no silent skipped range or duplicate outcome counts. |
| Full/disconnected destination or mount replacement | Stop with incomplete status; no writes to an unintended fallback path; surviving checkpoint is usable. |
| Dirty destination | No automatic repair or clean-health claim; select another destination or stop. |
| Truncated/hostile record, embedded command, path traversal | Resource bounds hold; no command execution, external access, or escape from output staging. |
| Duplicate-only findings | Zero novel complete records reported; acquisition completion remains distinct from original-file completeness. |
| Fragmented/unscoped findings | Preserve bytes and origins separately; do not invent names, attribution, chronology, or complete files. |
| Unsupported image layout | Analysis refuses or uses an explicitly validated adapter; packed spans are never silently treated as a contiguous image. |
| Restore-name collision | Export into fresh staging or report collision; no blind append/overwrite of existing files. |
| Boot on declared supported hardware | Input, source and destination devices work offline; guide remains usable without the original host or assistant. |
| Final report, sync, unmount | Independent hash/coverage replay agrees; removal is declared safe only after successful persistence and unmount. |

## Performance and correctness study

Use deterministic synthetic structured logs with a separate ground-truth ledger: intact files, overlapping snapshots, duplicates, unknown IDs, truncated records, records crossing chunk boundaries, and misleading embedded text. Place them in disposable ext4 images with known live/deleted extents and explicit gaps. Use a small fixture for iteration and a larger fixture exceeding the configured parser-memory bound for scaling. Preserve an immutable generated image, seed, hashes, expected byte spans and outcomes.

Compare the existing incident pipeline only if its source is made available and reviewed; otherwise label it unavailable and use the runbook/tool baseline. Do not import private captured logs into the fixture. Compare workflow variants first: identical bytes and extraction rules, changing one operation at a time. An alternative language prototype is a later experiment if profiling identifies a relevant CPU or memory limit.

Measure separately: boot/preparation time, operator interactions, bytes read, parse/hash/dedup time, writes and readback, peak memory, temporary disk use, checkpoint recovery time, and end-to-end time. Use the same tool versions, fixture, hardware and destination; record storage/filesystem and cache conditions. Run at least five repeated measured trials per condition, reporting median and range plus failures. Keep cold-start and warm-cache observations distinct; manipulate cache conditions only inside disposable environments.

Correctness is the entry gate: exact captured-span hashes, expected accepted/rejected record sets, identical baseline-relative novelty, preserved fragment origins, explicit omissions, and bounded resource behavior. Test an intentional one-byte corruption and a missing range to prove the checker detects them. Never trade away readback or provenance to make the benchmark faster.

A rewrite needs both equivalent results/safeguards and a material measured benefit. Proposed decision threshold: at least a 25% reduction in the dominant end-to-end workflow time or a demonstrated memory/packaging requirement the simpler path cannot meet. Parser microbenchmark gains alone do not satisfy that threshold. No benchmark was run during this discovery.

## Decision requested and handoff

Approve or revise the runbook-first milestone, technical Linux/ext4 audience, and 3–5 day exploratory budget. Select a separate project home before implementation; this epic currently holds the discovery record only. Do not create implementation slices until the maintainer has reviewed the proposal, as required by this issue's discovery acceptance criteria 3 and 6.

The incident lesson is routed to this epic: preserve a portable case record and measure workflow costs before proposing a new engine. The epic remains in progress pending scope review; it is not complete merely because this proposal exists. Subsequent implementation and hardware acceptance need their own scoped work after that decision.

title: Replace hand-rolled helpers with vim.* stdlib; collapse two local triplets
description:
Replace hand-rolled helpers with the Neovim stdlib the repo already uses
elsewhere, and collapse two file-local triplets. Found by a whole-repo
ponytail-audit on 2026-08-31.

Scope does NOT create a new generic utility boundary. Every item either deletes
toward an existing `vim.*` function or stays inside the file it is already in,
so louiselm-hu9i's standing rule ("do not centralize small Lua helpers merely
for deduplication if that creates a new generic utility boundary", reaffirmed in
louiselm-hu9i.4's rejection comment) does not bite here. Do not resolve any item
below by adding a `louiselm.util` module.

Replace with stdlib (`vim.split` is already used 4x and `vim.trim` 5x in this
repo, so these are inconsistency, not policy):

- Recursive `copy` duplicated verbatim: `session/registry.lua:72`,
  `session/lifecycle.lua:106`, `forensics/record.lua:29`,
  `workflow/escape.lua:9`. Shallow `copy`: `capture/init.lua:57`. Use
  `vim.deepcopy`.
- `copy_strings` duplicated verbatim: `permission/store.lua:68`,
  `routing/init.lua:23`, `routing/approval.lua:36`. Use `vim.deepcopy`.
- `split_lines` hand-rolled `find("\n")` loops: `ui/inline.lua:30`,
  `ui/diff/apply.lua:23`, `ui/chat/init.lua:1104`. Use
  `vim.split(value, "\n", { plain = true })`. NOTE: `ui/diff/apply.lua`'s
  variant returns a second value and its loop guard differs
  (`while start <= #value`), so it is NOT identical to the other two — check
  trailing-newline behavior against its callers before swapping.
- `trim`: `skills/metadata.lua:31`, `provenance/sources.lua:364`,
  `provenance/vintage.lua:35` (three different implementations). Use `vim.trim`.
- `contains` (`schema/gen_luacats.lua:33`) -> `vim.list_contains`. Skip if
  louiselm-luacats-generator-inert-5y8i deletes that file.
- `starts_with` (`skills/native_command.lua:45`) -> `vim.startswith`.
- `sorted_keys`: `agent/config.lua:82`, `schema/validate.lua:49` ->
  `vim.tbl_keys` + `table.sort`. The two sort comparators differ
  (`tostring` vs `key_sort_value`); keep each file's comparator.

Delete:

- `M.copy = Cache.copy` (`workflow/cache.lua:99`) — exported, zero callers
  repo-wide. The rest of cache.lua stays; it is a designed louiselm-qbr.8 slice
  per the Validation vocabulary record (louiselm-p5h0).
- `append_wrapped` duplicated verbatim with the same `MAX_WIDTH = 78` in
  `docs/vimdoc.lua:19` and `schema/gen_vimdoc.lua:64`. `docs/vimdoc.lua:1`
  already requires `gen_vimdoc`, so export the existing one rather than adding a
  module.

Collapse in place (no new files):

- `ui/provenance.lua:27,51,83` + `:102,110,118` — six functions, identical
  control flow, differing only in pattern and validator. One
  `token_at_cursor(line, column, pattern, validate)` and one
  `current_token(buffer, pattern, validate)`. Preserve the session-id variant's
  distinct behavior: it strips trailing punctuation, normalizes backticks, and
  measures the span against `raw_value` rather than `value`.
- `ui/chat/init.lua:248,273,318` — `copy_string_array`, `copy_skills`,
  `copy_initial_contexts` repeat the same dense-key check three times. One
  local `dense(value, label)` guard plus a per-item validator, file-local.

Estimated net about -250 lines, 0 dependency change.

Acceptance:
- Behavior-preserving; the diff/apply and session-id carve-outs above are
  covered by focused tests before the swap.
- No new module or utility boundary is introduced.
- `stylua --check .`, `lua-language-server --check . --checklevel=Warning`, the
  full mini.test suite, and `./scripts/generate-api-appendix --check` pass.
- Record the line delta in the close note.

comments.text:
Applied to every site where the file already depends on Neovim; skipped where it
does not. Net -94 lines (139 insertions, 233 deletions).

Applied:
- nvim.deepcopy replaces recursive/shallow `copy` in session/registry.lua,
  session/lifecycle.lua, capture/init.lua (18 call sites). Verified equivalent
  first: identical for plain data and for nil/scalars, differing only when a
  metatable is present, and all three copy plain table literals
  (lifecycle.lua:711 state, registry.lua:218, capture/init.lua:211 hold the
  metatables; the copied fields do not).
- nvim.trim replaces `trim` in provenance/sources.lua, provenance/vintage.lua.
- nvim.split(..., { plain = true }) replaces `split_lines` in ui/inline.lua and
  ui/chat/init.lua (13 call sites).
- Deleted the dead `M.copy` export in workflow/cache.lua.
- append_wrapped deduplicated: schema/gen_vimdoc.lua exports it, docs/vimdoc.lua
  consumes it through the require it already had, and its duplicate MAX_WIDTH is
  gone. `generate-vimdoc --check` passes byte-identical, which is the proof the
  dedupe changed nothing.
- ui/provenance.lua: extracted `only_match_at` and `current_token`, collapsing
  the shared tail of three cursor extractors and three identical cursor readers.
- ui/chat/init.lua: extracted `copy_dense`, collapsing the thrice-duplicated
  dense-key loop behind the three option copiers.

Not applied, and should not be:

- forensics/record.lua, workflow/escape.lua, permission/store.lua,
  routing/init.lua, routing/approval.lua, skills/metadata.lua,
  schema/gen_luacats.lua, skills/native_command.lua, agent/config.lua,
  schema/validate.lua. Around 44 modules reference Neovim nowhere -- neither
  `local nvim = vim` nor a bare `vim.` -- and they are exactly the pure layers.
  Introducing `vim.deepcopy`/`vim.trim`/`vim.startswith`/`vim.list_contains`
  there would trade a module's independence from the editor for five or six
  saved lines. This was not visible when the issue was written; the estimate of
  about -250 lines assumed all sites were eligible.
- ui/diff/apply.lua's `split_lines`. Filed as a carve-out to check; checking
  showed it is a genuine "do not". It returns `lines, trailing_newline` and
  pairs with `join_lines(lines, trailing_newline)`. vim.split encodes the
  trailing newline as a trailing empty element instead, so converting means
  detecting and popping that element and reworking join_lines -- more code, and
  it changes the empty-string case from `{}, true` to `{""}`.

Routed: AGENTS.md section 10 gained the Neovim-free-module rule, so the next
stdlib sweep does not have to rediscover the boundary. No follow-up issue filed
for the skipped sites: they are a decision not to do the work, not deferred work.

title: Parallel tool completions fragment chat folds
description: Observed in claude/272bb048-875f-4156-9b3f-28e7e1b85e3e and screenshot /home/lotso/Pictures/scrot/20260823_0408_943x1122_1787450923.png: one accidental subset of a tool-call paragraph is folded while neighboring completed calls stay expanded. The raw ACP log proves three parallel calls started in visual order A/B/C but completed B/C/A. chat/init.lua records completed lines in completion-event order and requires each new line to equal run.last + 1; a non-adjacent completion closes the run, so native folds depend on callback order rather than the rendered paragraph. Existing tests emit start/finish sequentially and miss parallel out-of-order completion. Acceptance: add a failing UI regression test with parallel starts and out-of-order finishes; after a prose chunk or turn_done, all contiguous completed tool lines in the rendered paragraph are one closed native fold regardless of completion order; failed and still-active calls remain unfolded; focused/full MiniTest, StyLua, and lua-language-server gates pass.
close_reason: Fixed tool folding to use rendered paragraph order; regression and all Lua gates pass

comments.author: codex/01a02c60-cf03-7eb2-8d6b-a4faa443c9e1
comments.text: Deeper reproduction from the same raw ACP log: each tool ID emits several non-terminal tool_call/tool_call_update events (Terminal, full command, shortened command). Chat currently appends every tool_call_started event and overwrites tool_lines[id], leaving prior started rows in the same visual paragraph. Sorting final completion rows alone would still not fold the screenshot. The regression therefore models repeated started updates plus B/C/A completion and requires the complete rendered paragraph to fold.

comments.author: codex/01a02c60-cf03-7eb2-8d6b-a4faa443c9e1
comments.text: Implemented paragraph-based folding: rendered tool lines are tracked as one contiguous paragraph, latest terminal status is tracked by tool ID, and paragraph closure creates folds only across completed-status spans. This makes repeated progress rows and out-of-order B/C/A completion fold together while failed/active IDs remain visible. title: Picker view shows only one visible entry despite multiple items
description:
## Summary

The picker view appears to contain only one visible entry, although its item count indicates that multiple items are available.

## Expected behavior

The picker should render enough of its list content for the available entries to be visibly distinguishable, with normal scrolling/navigation exposing the remaining items.

## Actual behavior

The view looks as if it has only one entry. The picker reports more items than are visibly displayed. The content rendered for an item may be too long and could be consuming the available display area.

## Ownership hypothesis

This may not be a louiselm rendering bug. Investigate whether the behavior comes from the snacks.nvim picker configuration/layout, item formatting, wrapping, height, or preview settings before changing louiselm.

## Reproduction

Open the affected louiselm picker and compare the visible entries with the picker-reported item count.

## Acceptance criteria

- Determine whether the root cause is louiselm or snacks.nvim configuration.
- If louiselm owns the issue, make multiple available entries visibly usable without breaking navigation.
- If snacks.nvim configuration owns it, document the required configuration change and avoid an unnecessary louiselm workaround.
notes: Root cause confirmed outside LouiseLM: the active Snacks configuration sets picker.win.list.wo.wrap=true globally. LouiseLM passes distinct choices through vim.ui.select; wrapped long rows consume the select layout height. README documents a picker.sources.select win.list.wo.wrap=false override, verified against the installed Snacks config merge. No provider-specific LouiseLM workaround added.
close_reason: Confirmed Snacks list wrapping as root cause and documented the source-scoped configuration fix

title: Restyle README hero with mural print aesthetic
description:
## Goal
Restyle the existing README hero so it uses the supplied mural reference visual language while preserving the current LouiseLM composition, spirit, and symbols.

## Scope
- In scope: replace `assets/louiselm-hero.webp` in place, using `/home/lotso/Downloads/1786245984429.jpg` as the visual reference.
- Preserve the existing landscape composition and recognizable motifs: the central portrait; connected mesh; people writing, coding, organizing, and speaking; the books, cubes, leaf, microphone, waveform, raised fists, megaphone, birds, and building.
- Apply a strict white, black, and red treatment: a clearer neutral or slightly warm white instead of the current beige/parchment cast; dense near-black ink; and vivid deep-red accents.
- Give the black artwork the reference mural character: rough hand-printed woodcut or engraved linework, cross-hatching and stippling, imperfect ink coverage, distressed contours, and slight registration/edge irregularity. Keep enough contrast and detail for README display size.
- Retain subtle physical surface or print texture, but do not let it muddy the white ground or read as yellowed paper.
- Out of scope: changing README copy, image placement, alt text, core composition, adding unrelated symbols, or turning the scene into a photograph of a building/mural.

## Acceptance Criteria

title: HostIdentity Sessions cannot write their private directories
description:
A Bubblewrap Session running under its assigned host UID cannot write the private home or workspace that isolation evidence promises are writable.

## Observed

2026-09-03 code inspection while implementing louiselm-i03a. `skills-core/src/sandbox.rs:708-713` creates both directories as the privileged launcher but never changes ownership. After `CommandExt::uid/gid` correctly drops Bubblewrap to the assigned identity, those root-owned `0755` leaves are not writable by the Session.

## Symptoms

- The Agent cannot create files in its HOME or working directory after host-identity isolation is enabled.
- Isolation evidence still says both locations are private and writable.

## Root cause

Directory materialization and identity application are split without transferring ownership at their shared backend boundary.

## Why it was not caught

All real Bubblewrap tests use `IdentityPlan::NamespaceOnly`, where the launcher and Session share the owner UID.

## Fix direction

When materializing a `HostIdentity` plan, assign the newly created home and workspace leaves to the planned UID/GID before spawn. Keep pool allocation and exclusive UID leasing in louiselm-d6fv.4.2/.4.

## Acceptance

- A privileged/user-namespace regression runs under an assigned non-root host UID and writes both private directories.
- Namespace-only behavior is unchanged.
- Rust format, clippy, and full tests pass.

## Not covered

Recursive repair of caller-populated directory trees and identity-pool installation remain outside this backend fix.

title: Sync now waits behind hours-long upload backoff
description:
Tapping Sync now while the unique upload chain is retrying does not make an immediate upload attempt. The new request is appended behind the backed-off work, so a user who has restored connectivity can remain stuck for hours despite explicitly asking to sync.

## Observed

Physical Android QA for louiselm-qbr.1.9 on 2026-08-21, Xiaomi 21081111RG, app 0.1.0, workstation and phone on 192.168.10.0/24.

After the user confirmed `Paired with https://192.168.10.121:7391`, tapped Sync now, and still saw `6 capture(s) waiting locally`, `adb shell dumpsys jobscheduler dev.louiselm.capture` reported:

```
Minimum latency: +3h10m0s129ms
Required constraints: TIMING_DELAY CONNECTIVITY
Satisfied constraints: CONNECTIVITY DEVICE_NOT_DOZING BACKGROUND_NOT_RESTRICTED TARE_WEALTH WITHIN_QUOTA
Unsatisfied constraints: TIMING_DELAY
```

The receiver still contained 4 captures, and none of the 6 pending phone captures gained upload state or an uploaded marker.

## Symptoms

- The user taps Sync now, but the visible waiting count remains 6.
- Android reports validated Wi-Fi connectivity but defers the worker for more than three hours.

## Root cause

`android/app/src/main/java/dev/louiselm/capture/UploadWorker.kt:42-50` routes every trigger through `enqueueUniqueWork(..., ExistingWorkPolicy.APPEND_OR_REPLACE, request)`. A manual request is appended behind the existing retry chain, preserving its exponential-backoff timing instead of running now.

## Why it was not caught

The Android tests cover protocol and storage behavior, but do not distinguish automatic retry scheduling from the user-initiated Sync now action or inspect unique-work policy.

## Fix direction

Separate the manual-sync scheduling policy from ordinary automatic enqueue. Manual sync should replace/cancel backed-off unique work and enqueue a connected-network request immediately; automatic capture/pair triggers should retain normal retry coalescing. Keep one upload worker and one unique-work name.

## Acceptance

- A regression test fails before the fix and proves manual sync selects an immediate replacement policy while automatic enqueue retains retry-safe coalescing.
- With a real backed-off worker and restored Wi-Fi, tapping Sync now causes an immediate receiver request.
- Pending captures upload under their original UUIDs without duplicates.

## Not covered

Automatic exponential backoff timing itself and OEM-specific WorkManager scheduling beyond the connected Xiaomi device are not changed.
close_reason: Fixed in 43aaa9b. Manual Sync now replaces backed-off unique work while automatic triggers retain retry coalescing. Regression: UploadWorkerTest.manualSyncReplacesBackedOffUploadWork failed before and passed after. Physical Xiaomi retest uploaded all six queued UUIDs immediately, raised receiver count 4 to 10, preserved each UUID, and left zero attention. Gates: Gradle test/lint/assembleDebug, 315 mini.test cases, StyLua, and lua-language-server all pass.
